source.body_excerpt: Addresses usually have abbreviations and contractions. Do not add punctuation marks to these.
heading_path: Use shortened forms for addresses
source.statement: Use shortened forms for addresses

source.body_excerpt: Names of buildings, structures and public places have initial capitals. Write generic and plural terms in lower case.
heading_path: Write the names of buildings, structures and public places with an initial capital
source.statement: Write the names of buildings, structures and public places with an initial capital

source.body_excerpt:
Spell out the names of Australian states and territories in formal content.

You can use shortened forms when:

- the name is used as an adjective
- space is limited
- the full name would result in repetition
- you are writing an address.
heading_path: Shorten names for states and territories in 4 situations
source.statement: Shorten names for states and territories in 4 situations

source.body_excerpt: Use initial capitals for trade marks, brands and business names.
heading_path: Use initial capitals for commercial terms
source.statement: Use initial capitals for commercial terms

source.body_excerpt: Avoid using trade marks and brand names if possible. Instead use a generic word.
heading_path: Use a common word for a product if you can
source.statement: Use a common word for a product if you can

violating_examples: Kleenex
Esky

source.body_excerpt: A few words have different meanings when used as a trade mark or used generically.
heading_path: Take care using product names
A product name can change meaning when used in the generic sense
source.statement: A product name can change meaning when used in the generic sense

source.body_excerpt:
Use initial capitals only for the formal names and titles of government entities and office holders. Use lower case for generic references.

These are rules for general content. There might be exceptions if you are writing specialist legal content using terms defined in legislation.

This page orders guidance for common government terms alphabetically.
heading_path: Use initial capitals for formal names and titles
source.statement: Use initial capitals for formal names and titles

source.body_excerpt:
Use an initial capital letter for medical terms only if the term is a proper noun or adjective, or if it is the name of a genus. Otherwise don’t use initial capitals for the names of:

- diseases and viruses
- diagnostic procedures
- syndromes
- anatomical parts.
heading_path: Use capitals for proper nouns and genus names
source.statement: Use capitals for proper nouns and genus names

source.body_excerpt: Write scientific names of infectious organisms – such as viruses, bacteria and parasites – in italics. Use an initial capital for the name of the genus only.
heading_path: Italicise organism names
source.statement: Italicise organism names

source.body_excerpt:
Use the generic names of drugs where possible. Write them in lower case.

You can include the brand name in parentheses after the common name. Use initial capitals for brand names. Commercial terms might be trade marked: take care [using product names](/node/89#take_care_using_product_names).
heading_path: Cite common names for pharmaceutical drugs, not brand names
source.statement: Cite common names for pharmaceutical drugs, not brand names

compliant_examples: People with pneumonia-like infections might have Legionnaires’ disease (*legionellosis*).

source.body_excerpt:
The language you use for some medical conditions can change as research and social understanding of the conditions evolve. Be mindful of outdated language that can perpetuate stigma or misunderstandings about the condition.

Refer to peak bodies that study the condition or that provide support and information to people affected by it.
heading_path: Refer to medical conditions using clear and inclusive language
source.statement: Refer to medical conditions using clear and inclusive language

violating_examples: a cancer patient
Asthma sufferers
a diabetic person

If you’re writing both the scientific and common names for a medical condition, place the scientific name in parentheses. Don’t use ‘or’. This could confuse readers into thinking they are 2 separate medical conditions.
People with pneumonia-like infections might have Legionnaires’ disease or *legionellosis*.

source.body_excerpt:
Some countries have several official names. Consult trusted references to decide which name to use, then use it consistently. Helpful references include:

- the
[countries, economies and regions](https://www.dfat.gov.au/geo/pages/countries-and-regions)webpages, on the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade website - the United Nations
[geographical names database](https://unstats.un.org/unsd/geoinfo/geonames/) - the Australian Bureau of Statistics
.*Standard Australian classification of countries*
heading_path: Check official sources for country and place names
source.statement: Check official sources for country and place names

source.body_excerpt:
Use initial capitals for:

- the official name of a country
- any commonly used short forms of the country’s name
- the names of states, territories and provinces.

The definite article ‘the’ isn’t capitalised unless it begins a sentence.
heading_path: Spell country names with a capital letter
source.statement: Spell country names with a capital letter

source.body_excerpt: Use a short form of a country’s name only if it’s clear and accurate. Shortened forms can make it easier to read text or tables, illustrations, notes, lists and bibliographies.
heading_path: Shorten a country name only if it is clear to the user
source.statement: Shorten a country name only if it is clear to the user

source.body_excerpt: English-language content usually uses the English version of a country’s name.
heading_path: Use English versions of countries and places in most content
source.statement: Use English versions of countries and places in most content

source.body_excerpt: Groups of nations or areas that are recognised as political or geographic regions take initial capitals.
heading_path: Check the official status for area and region names
source.statement: Check the official status for area and region names

source.body_excerpt: There’s usually a clear relationship between the name of the country or region and the word used for the nationality. It’s not always obvious though, so check a dictionary to ensure you’re using the correct term.
heading_path: Write nationalities, peoples and places with initial capitals
source.statement: Write nationalities, peoples and places with initial capitals

source.body_excerpt: The name of a country’s language isn’t always derived from the name of the country.
heading_path: Check if an official language differs from the country name
source.statement: Check if an official language differs from the country name

source.body_excerpt:
Scientific terms for natural phenomena can include common nouns that combine to form a proper noun.

Use initial capitals when spelling out this kind of scientific term. Common shortened forms are in full capitals. Any non-English names retain the spelling of the original.
heading_path: Terms for specific phenomena can take initial capitals
source.statement: Terms for specific phenomena can take initial capitals

source.body_excerpt:
Organisations determine how their names should be spelt and punctuated. This does not always follow the usual rules.

Write the name of the organisation the same way the organisation writes it. This rule applies except in rare cases when the organisation name is in all lower case. Use an initial capital for these names in body text. This helps people identify the name as a proper noun.

Some names start with a lower case letter but have a medial capital (for example, ‘eBay’). Write the name the same way, including to begin a sentence. A medial capital is enough to identify the name as a proper noun.
heading_path: Write the name as the organisation writes it
source.statement: Write the name as the organisation writes it

source.body_excerpt:
The names of organisations can change. The most efficient way to confirm an organisation’s name is to check its website, annual report or letterhead. If this is unsuccessful, there are other reliable services.

For Australian Government entities, use the [government online directory](https://www.directory.gov.au/). Directory entries contain links to departmental pages listing annual reports. Annual reports are a good way to find the former names of departments.

The government online directory includes the Australian Government Organisations Register and the directories of state and territory governments. There are also website directories for some local governments.

For non-government entities, use:

- the Australian Securities Exchange's
[listed companies](https://www.asx.com.au/asx/research/listedCompanies.do) - the
[Australian Securities and Investments Commission registers](https://connectonline.asic.gov.au/RegistrySearch/faces/landing/SearchRegisters.jspx?_adf.ctrl-state=p64f240em_12)

For all entities, use:

- the Australian Business Register's
[ABN lookup](https://abr.business.gov.au/) - a publication that lists organisations such as the
*Directory of Australian associatio
heading_path: Check the correct name of an organisation
source.statement: Check the correct name of an organisation

source.body_excerpt:
Use initial capitals for:

- all words capitalised in the full, official names of organisations
- the first mention of an organisation.

Don’t use an initial capital for:

- generic terms – such as ‘the department’
or ‘the agency’ – even if the organisation being referenced capitalises the generic term in its content - mentions of several organisations with the same generic name.
heading_path: Capitalise organisations’ names in 2 situations
source.statement: Capitalise organisations' names in 2 situations

source.body_excerpt: Use an apostrophe only when it forms part of the official name of an organisation.
heading_path: Put a possessive apostrophe in a name if the organisation does
source.statement: Put a possessive apostrophe in a name if the organisation does

compliant_examples: The Bureau of Meteorology has been quick to respond.
Woolworths is advertising its new stock.
NT Fisheries has reviewed its policies.

source.body_excerpt:
The rules of grammar allow the use of a plural or singular verb with the names of organisations. This is not Australian Government style.

Always use a singular verb. This applies even if organisation names end in an ‘s’* *and look plural.
heading_path: Use the singular verb with organisation names
source.statement: Use the singular verb with organisation names

violating_examples: The Bureau of Meteorology have been quick to respond.
Woolworths are advertising their new stock.
The United Nations turn 75 in 2020.
NT Fisheries have reviewed their policies.

source.body_excerpt:
When you write to or about people, always use the form of personal name that the person uses. If you can, ask the person which name they prefer. Otherwise, consult reputable sources for:

- Names of people who work within government or in roles related to government, including state and territory governments:
[Directory.gov.au](https://www.directory.gov.au/). - Records of names of people closely associated with Australia: The
[National Archives of Australia](https://www.naa.gov.au/help-your-research/getting-started/commonwealth-record-series-crs-system). - Historical and biographical information: The
and*Australian dictionary of biography*[Trove](https://trove.nla.gov.au/). - Information on prominent Australians, search ‘eResources’ such as
*Who*’*s who in Australia*or*Encyclopedia Britannica:*[National Library of Australia](https://www.nla.gov.au/)*.* - The accepted form of authors’ names and the names of people being written about: library catalogues.

Names are important to a person’s sense of self. To avoid cultural or gender bias when referring to parts of names, use:

- ‘given name’ instead of ‘Christian name’
- ‘family name’ instead of ‘surname’
- ‘previous names’ instead of
heading_path: Use the right name
source.statement: Use the right name

source.body_excerpt: Use initial capitals for the names of real and fictitious people.
heading_path: Use initial capitals for personal names, initials and nicknames
source.statement: Use initial capitals for personal names, initials and nicknames

source.body_excerpt:
The plural of any personal name is formed by adding ‘s’ or ‘es’. It depends on the spelling of the personal name (Table 1).

| Names ending in | Action to make plural | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| ‘s’, ‘x’ and ‘z’ | Add ‘es’ | There were 3 Yanises and 2 Lizes at the meeting but no Alexes. |
| ‘y’ | Keep the ‘y’ and add ‘s’ | The Murphys always meet on Tuesdays. |
| ‘i’ | Keep the ‘i’ and add ‘s’ | The 2 Ranis were close colleagues. |
| ‘o’ | Add an ‘s’ | The 4 young Angelos played together all day. |
| All other letters | Add an ‘s’ | The 2 Evelyns in the section were cousins. |
heading_path: Spell plural forms correctly
source.statement: Spell plural forms correctly

source.body_excerpt:
Use an apostrophe and an ‘s’ with personal names, even when they already end in ‘s’ (Table 2).

Plural personal names take just an apostrophe. Simply add an apostrophe to the end of the plural form.

| Number | Names ending in | Action to show possessive case | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Singular (one person) | ‘s’ | Add apostrophe ‘s’ (’s) | Jas’s report |
| Singular (one person) | Any letter other than ‘s’ | Add apostrophe ‘s’ (’s) | Tui’s signature |
| Plural (2 or more people of the same name) | The plural ‘s’ or ‘es’ | Add only an apostrophe (’) without an extra ‘s’ | The Joneses’ responses or the Nasrins’ name tags |
| Plural (2 or more people of a different name) | Any letter other than ‘s’ | Add only an apostrophe ‘s’ (’s) on the last name | Aiko and Tashi’s team |
| Plural (2 or more people using singular pronoun and possessive pronoun with a noun) | Any letter other than ‘s’ | Add only an apostrophe ‘s’ (’s) on the noun | You and your partner’s luggage |
heading_path: Punctuate possessive forms with an apostrophe
source.statement: Punctuate possessive forms with an apostrophe

source.body_excerpt: Always retain hyphens when you write given and family names that are hyphenated.
heading_path: Keep hyphens and all parts of compound family names
source.statement: Keep hyphens and all parts of compound family names

source.body_excerpt: As far as possible, if you need to write a non-English name, use the same form and spelling as the person uses. Check their personal correspondence or works they have written. If you can, ask them how you should address them. As a last resort, use the name that is most commonly used in writing about the person.
heading_path: Follow reliable sources for non-English names
source.statement: Follow reliable sources for non-English names

source.body_excerpt:
Given and family names sometimes have diacritic marks or symbols, including accents, such as à, á, â, ã, ä, ė, ē, ĕ, ę.

When you write names, retain diacritic marks unless the person commonly uses a simplified form of their name.

Insert diacritic marks into your document with the [Unicode Standard](https://www.unicode.org/charts/) – for example, U+00E8 is è. In word processing applications, you can also use the [ASCII extended character set](https://www.ascii-code.com).
heading_path: Follow reliable sources for non-English names
Keep accents and diacritic marks in names
source.statement: Keep accents and diacritic marks in names

source.body_excerpt:
Some family names contain a particle, such as ‘della’, ‘Al’ or ‘von’.

It is sometimes difficult to decide how to capitalise these personal names in English.

Use the same capitalisation as the person uses. It is largely a matter of individual preference and family custom. If you can’t ask them, use reliable resources to decide on a case-by-case basis, then use the same form throughout the content.

Most, but not all, particles are written in lower case.
heading_path: Follow reliable sources for non-English names
Treat names with particles case by case
source.statement: Treat names with particles case by case

source.body_excerpt:
In a reference list, put the family name first and then the initial for the given name of the lead author.

Follow the rules for the author–date system to [create an alphabetically ordered list](/node/165#alphabetise_the_reference_items_in_the_list).

Names you pronounce the same way but spell differently go together in an alphabetical list.
heading_path: List family name first in reference lists
source.statement: List family name first in reference lists

source.body_excerpt:
The genus and species form the definitive name of a plant or animal. By convention:

- the genus is in italics and takes an initial capital
- the species is in italics and is lower case.
heading_path: Italicise genus and species names
source.statement: Italicise genus and species names

source.body_excerpt:
Most plants and animals have a common name as well as their genus and species name.

For common names:

- Use lower case unless they are also a proper noun, a registered trade mark or in some specialised content such as genetics.
- Do not use italics.
heading_path: Write common names in lower case and roman type
source.statement: Write common names in lower case and roman type

source.body_excerpt:
The common name of a plant or animal can be a local name for more than one species in different places. Only the scientific name is the definitive name.

For this reason, include the species name in parentheses when you first mention the common name so it is clear which plant or animal you are writing about.
heading_path: Include the genus and species at first mention of the common name
source.statement: Include the genus and species at first mention of the common name

source.body_excerpt: If you have already written the full name of the genus, use a shortened form for later mentions. This is often just the first letter of the genus name, followed by a full stop. This is an exception to the [general rule for abbreviations](/node/184#dont_put_a_full_stop_after_most_abbreviations).
heading_path: Include the genus and species at first mention of the common name
When the genus is repeated, it can be abbreviated
source.statement: When the genus is repeated, it can be abbreviated

source.body_excerpt:
Plants and animals are classified in a hierarchy from general to specific. The style you use is set by where the name is in the hierarchy:

- Names down to genus level start with capital letters.
- Species names are in lower case.
- Genus and species names are in italics.

The examples in the table show the classification for:

- a plant, lemon-scented myrtle
- an animal, the platypus.

| Classification terms | Lemon-scented myrtle (botany) |
|---|---|
| Kingdom | Plantae |
| Division | Tracheophyta |
| Order | Myrtales |
| Family | Myrtaceae |
| Genus | Backhousia |
| Species | Backhousia citriodora |

| Classification terms | Platypus (zoology) |
|---|---|
| Kingdom | Animalia |
| Phylum | Chordata |
| Class | Mammalia |
| Order | Monotremata |
| Family | Ornithorhynchidae |
| Genus | Ornithorhynchus |
| Species | Ornithorhynchus anatinus |
heading_path: Refer to classification systems to help you name plants and animals
source.statement: Refer to classification systems to help you name plants and animals

source.body_excerpt:
Technical content often includes the name of the person who first described the species.

The person's name follows the first mention of the species in the content. The publishing date of the description can also follow the name.

The name and date, if they are included, appear in roman type.
heading_path: Refer to classification systems to help you name plants and animals
Scientific names can include the name of a person
source.statement: Scientific names can include the name of a person

source.body_excerpt:
Check the names of plants and animals. Make sure the information is up to date.

Use reliable sources such as:
heading_path: Use specialised resources for more information
source.statement: Use specialised resources for more information

source.body_excerpt:
Write the names of individual ships, aircraft and other vehicles:

- in italics
- with initial capitals.

This makes the name of the ship, aircraft or other vehicle clear. The name contrasts with the rest of the sentence.

Don't use the definite article for navy ships.
heading_path: Italicise specific names and use capitals
source.statement: Italicise specific names and use capitals

source.body_excerpt: Begin the names of the brands, models and classes of vehicles with an initial capital letter but don’t use italics.
heading_path: Don’t write brands or types of vehicles in italics
source.statement: Don't write brands or types of vehicles in italics

source.body_excerpt: Use the pronoun ‘it’ for ships, aircraft and other vehicles. Do not write ‘she’ when referring to vehicles in government content. Use pronouns that reflect [gender-neutral language](/node/64#use_genderneutral_language).
heading_path: Refer to vehicles with the pronoun ‘it’
source.statement: Refer to vehicles with the pronoun 'it'

source.body_excerpt:
Check official place names and [style them correctly](/node/134). You can check the spelling of an official name using the [Australian Place Names dataset](https://placenames.fsdf.org.au/).

The full names of mountains, rivers, valleys, bays, islands and other features always take initial capitals.
heading_path: Write official names with capitals
source.statement: Write official names with capitals

source.body_excerpt: In most cases, don’t use initial capitals when you use the name as a generic term.
heading_path: Write generic terms in lower case
source.statement: Write generic terms in lower case

source.body_excerpt: ‘Mt’* *is a common and easily recognisable abbreviation for mountains. Use the abbreviation consistently in content and use initial capitals.
heading_path: Limit abbreviated names
source.statement: Limit abbreviated names

source.body_excerpt:
Don’t use an apostrophe for topographic terms involving possessives. Official place names are not possessive and do not usually include punctuation.

Refer to related [guidance on Australian place names](/node/134#check_official_place_names_and_style_them_correctly).
heading_path: Don’t use an apostrophe for possessive names
source.statement: Don't use an apostrophe for possessive names

violating_examples: Carey’s Peak

source.body_excerpt: The plural of any topographic name is formed simply by adding ‘s’ or ‘es’.
heading_path: Spell the plural form correctly
source.statement: Spell the plural form correctly

source.body_excerpt: In text, write the points of a compass in lower case. Use hyphens for points such as ‘north-east’.
heading_path: Write compass points in lower case
source.statement: Write compass points in lower case

compliant_examples: Only one person agreed to it.
Their aim is zero net emissions by 2050.
They were open to discussing 3 options.

source.body_excerpt:
In text, the general rule is:

- Use numerals for ‘2’ and above.
- Write the numbers ‘zero’ and ‘one’ in words.

Follow the same rule for writing numbers in [headings and subheadings](/node/51). Apply exceptions to this general rule in specific situations, explained on this page.

The numbers ‘0’ and ‘1’ are difficult for some users to read. Some typefaces make it difficult to see the difference between:

- the letter ‘O’ and numeral ‘0’
- the letters ‘I’ (capital ‘i’), ‘l’ (lower-case ‘L’) and numeral ‘1’.

In some typefaces, the numeral ‘1’ can also be confused with the numeral ‘7’.

Writing ‘zero’ and ‘one’ helps to ensure all users understand you are referring to the number.
heading_path: Use numerals for 2 and above in text
source.statement: Use numerals for 2 and above in text

violating_examples: Only 1 person agreed with it.
Their aim is 0 net emissions by 2050.
They were open to discussing three options.

source.body_excerpt:
There are exceptions to the general rule for using numerals in text.

Use words for numbers when:

- starting a sentence
- writing a fraction
- writing a proper noun that includes a number written as a word
- writing a publication title that includes a number written as a word
- quoting a figure of speech.

In addition, use words for numbers below 10 for government content that follows journalistic conventions (for example, media releases).
heading_path: Use words for 2 and above in these specific situations
source.statement: Use words for 2 and above in these specific situations

source.body_excerpt:
There are exceptions to using words for ‘zero’ and ‘one’.

Write all numbers as numerals:

- in units of measurement
- to show mathematical relationships – such as equations and ratios – and for decimals
- when you are comparing numbers
- in tables and charts
- for dates and times
- in a series of numbers
- in specific contexts – such as steps, instructions, age and school years
- in scientific content.
heading_path: Write all numbers as numerals in these specific situations
source.statement: Write all numbers as numerals in these specific situations

compliant_examples: The government awards 2,500 grants to community projects annually.

source.body_excerpt: Numbers from 1,000 need a [comma](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/punctuation-and-capitalisation/commas). Separate the digits into groups of 3 (working from right to left).
heading_path: Use commas in numbers with 4 or more digits
source.statement: Use commas in numbers with 4 or more digits

violating_examples: The government awards 2 500 grants to community projects annually.

source.body_excerpt:
Numbers below a million are easy to read as numerals. When you’re using rounded numbers of 1,000 or more, [use commas to separate numerals into groups of 3](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/punctuation/commas#use_commas_in_numbers_with_4_or_more_digits) (working right to left).

Use a combination of numerals and words for large numbers from a million when they are rounded. It is easier to read ‘2.5 million’ than ‘2,500,000’.
heading_path: Combine numerals and words for large, rounded numbers
source.statement: Combine numerals and words for large, rounded numbers

source.body_excerpt: Both forms are acceptable in government content. Choosing which style to use will depend on the context and the type of content.
heading_path: Use ‘1 million’ and ‘one million’ in certain contexts
source.statement: Use '1 million' and 'one million' in certain contexts

heading_path: Choose between numerals or words for currency
source.statement: Choose between numerals or words for currency

heading_path: Reference non-Australian currencies for accessibility
source.statement: Reference non-Australian currencies for accessibility

source.body_excerpt: Use words for amounts of money that are an expression rather than an actual amount.
heading_path: Use words for inexact amounts
source.statement: Use words for inexact amounts

source.body_excerpt:
There are Australian conventions for writing dates in words and numerals, and in numeric formats. These conventions include how to sequence elements of the date.

Use numerals and words for dates in most content. Use numeric dates when space is limited and in content types like tables.
heading_path: Follow Australian conventions for dates
source.statement: Follow Australian conventions for dates

compliant_examples: Please find attached the new agenda for the extraordinary general meeting, 2 pm 8 November 2022.
Schedule 3 commences on the first 1 July after the bill receives Royal Assent.

source.body_excerpt:
In Australia, the conventional sequence for dates is ‘day month year’. Use this sequence when expressing dates in numerals and words.

For dates in body text, use numerals for the day and year and spell out the name of the month. Don’t include a comma or any other punctuation.

Spell out the name of the day if it is being used, but don’t include a comma after the day.

The names of months and days start with an initial capital because they are [proper nouns](//www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/types-words/nouns#proper_nouns_are_the_names_of_people_and_specific_things”).
heading_path: Combine numerals and words for dates in body text
source.statement: Combine numerals and words for dates in body text

violating_examples: December 31, 2020
Thursday, 31 December 2020
Insert a non-breaking space between the day and the month so they stay together on one line. A non-breaking space means that a line break will split the date before the year.
Keeping the day and month together allows people to identify the information appearing before the line break as a date.
Please find attached the draft minutes of the extraordinary general meeting held in Sydney, 8 November 2022.
Don’t use an ordinal number (12th, 21st etc.) when writing dates in body text.
1st May 1997
Schedule 3 commences on the first 1st July after the bill receives Royal Assent.

source.body_excerpt:
Only use abbreviations if space is limited – for example, in tables, illustrations, charts and notes. Ensure that it is obvious to users which days of the week or months you are referring to.

The standard abbreviations for the days of the week are:

- Monday – ‘Mon’ or ‘M’
- Tuesday – ‘Tues’ (‘Tue’) or ‘Tu’
- Wednesday – ‘Wed’ or ‘W’
- Thursday – 'Thurs’ (‘Thur’,‘Thu’) or ‘Th’
- Friday – ‘Fri’ or ‘F’
- Saturday – ‘Sat’ or ‘Sa’
- Sunday – ‘Sun’ or ‘Su’.

The abbreviations in parentheses are alternatives for the standard abbreviation they follow. Only use the alternatives when the context ensures their meaning is clear.

Note: Style Manual lists Monday as the first day of the week. This is consistent with the order of calendar days in a calendar week as defined in the [international standard adopted by Australia](#IntlCom).

The standard abbreviations for the months are:

- January – ‘Jan’
- February – ‘Feb’
- March – ‘Mar’
- April – ‘Apr’
- May – retain as ‘May’
- June – retain as ‘June’ or shorten to ‘Jun’
- July – retain as ‘July’ or shorten to ‘Jul’
- August – ‘Aug’
- September – ‘Sept’ or shorten to ‘Sep’
- October – ‘Oct’
- November – ‘Nov’
- December – ‘Dec’.

Only use the sh
heading_path: Use shortened forms for dates when space is limited
source.statement: Use shortened forms for dates when space is limited

compliant_examples: The Labor Party called an urgent conference on Saturday 22 December.

source.body_excerpt: Avoid abbreviated words when writing dates in body text. Words written in full are usually easier to read and understand.
heading_path: Use shortened forms for dates when space is limited
Don’t abbreviate dates in body text
source.statement: Don't abbreviate dates in body text

violating_examples: The Labor Party called an urgent conference on Sat 22 Dec.

source.body_excerpt:
Avoid writing dates entirely in numerals for general content. Use numeric dates only when space is limited (such as in tables).

Numeric dates can be confusing because their order and format differs between countries.

Use Australia’s conventional order of ‘day month year’ unless you are writing for users in a country that uses a different style.
heading_path: Don’t write dates as numerals unless space is limited
source.statement: Don't write dates as numerals unless space is limited

source.body_excerpt: Separate the numbers in a numeric date with an unspaced forward slash, using the format ‘day/month/year’. This format uses single digits for single-digit days and months.
heading_path: Don’t write dates as numerals unless space is limited
Use a forward slash in numeric dates
source.statement: Use a forward slash in numeric dates

source.body_excerpt:
You can also use 2 digits for each element.

Only use this style for the year:

- in financial data
- if it is clear which century you are referring to
- if users understand the order of the elements (‘day month year’ for Australian users).
heading_path: Don’t write dates as numerals unless space is limited
Numeric dates can have 2-digit elements
source.statement: Numeric dates can have 2-digit elements

source.body_excerpt: Write decades with an ‘s’ on the end. Don’t use an [apostrophe](/node/106) to show the plural.
heading_path: Don’t use an apostrophe for decades
source.statement: Don't use an apostrophe for decades

violating_examples: In more casual writing, you can use expressions such as ‘the eighties’. You can also use an apostrophe to show the missing numerals in a decade – for example, ‘In the ’80s, all my jackets had shoulder pads.’

source.body_excerpt:
As a general rule, write spans of years in words, using ‘to’, ‘from … to’ or ‘between … and’. Write the years out in full, not as abbreviations.

Don’t replace the word between the years with an [en dash](//www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/punctuation/dashes).
heading_path: Use words for spans of years in body text
source.statement: Use words for spans of years in body text

violating_examples: the years 2015–2019
between 2015–2019

compliant_examples: Australia’s energy consumption rose by 0.6% in 2018–19 and fell by 2.9% in 2019–20.

source.body_excerpt:
Government content often includes spans of years. Some year spans are easier to read and understand if they contain an unspaced en dash rather than words.

This is particularly true in content that contains multiple spans of years. In this case, using en dashes makes the content easier to scan.

Use an unspaced en dash for a:

- financial year
- calendar year
- span of years in the titles of publications and programs
- span of years written in parentheses, such as for a term of office and the years of birth and death.

Always include the phrases ‘financial year’, ‘financial years’, ‘calendar year’ or ‘calendar years’ unless the context makes the meaning clear. You can also introduce the relevant phrase at first mention and just write the year span, without the phrase, in later mentions.

Finally, exercise your judgement. Consider using en dashes for year spans when using words makes the content harder to read.
heading_path: Use en dashes for particular types of year spans
source.statement: Use en dashes for particular types of year spans

violating_examples: National Road Safety Action Plan 2018/20
Australia’s energy consumption rose by 0.6% in 2018/19 and fell by 2.9% in 2019/20.

source.body_excerpt:
As a general rule, use ‘from … to’ and ‘between … and’ in spans of days and months.

If it’s appropriate for your content, keep elements of the span together by inserting [non-breaking spaces](#NonBreakSpace) between them.

When you include a year, insert a non-breaking space between the day and month. A non-breaking space keeps the day and month together while the line break splits the date before the year.
heading_path: Use words for spans of days and months in body text
source.statement: Use words for spans of days and months in body text

source.body_excerpt:
Only use en dashes for spans of days and months if you have limited space. This could be in display text, tables, lists or in social media posts.

But also exercise your judgement – consider using en dashes if using words makes the content harder to read.

The en dash is spaced when the day and month appear on both sides of the span.
heading_path: Use en dashes for spans of days and months when space is limited
source.statement: Use en dashes for spans of days and months when space is limited

source.body_excerpt:
Treat specific days, public events and periods in history as proper nouns and use initial capitals. Use lower case for ‘the’ and any [prepositions](/node/130), unless they are capitalised as part of a proprietary name.

In body text, use lower case for generic terms like the names of seasons –‘autumn’ – and astronomical events such as ‘equinox’ and ‘solstice’. Write ‘century’ and ‘centuries’ in lower case.
heading_path: Refer to specific days, events and periods with capitals
source.statement: Refer to specific days, events and periods with capitals

source.body_excerpt:
In most documents, numerals give a clearer expression of time. Write times of day using numerals, especially when you need to convey precise times.

Use a colon between the hours and minutes. The use of a colon as the separator, rather than a full stop, reflects a shift in contemporary Australian usage.

A colon ensures that the time isn’t confused with a decimal number.

For example, ‘10.50’ can be read as ‘10 and a half’ as well as ‘50 minutes past 10’. Screen reader users will probably hear ‘10.50’ as ‘10 point 5’.
heading_path: Use numerals for times of day
source.statement: Use numerals for times of day

source.body_excerpt:
Only use en dashes for time spans if you have limited space. This could be in display text, tables, lists or in social media posts.

But also exercise your judgement – consider using en dashes if using words makes the content harder to read.

The spacing of the en dash depends on the elements of the span.

Use an unspaced en dash:

- if the ‘am’ or ‘pm’ appears only at the end of the span
- for spans of time in the 24-hour clock format.

Use a spaced en dash:

- when ‘am’ or ‘pm’ appears on both sides of the span
- if ‘noon’, ‘midday’ or ‘midnight’ appears in the span.
heading_path: Use en dashes for spans of time when space is limited
source.statement: Use en dashes for spans of time when space is limited

source.body_excerpt:
When expressing duration (lengths of time) in body text, follow Style Manual rules about [choosing words or numerals](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/numbers-and-measurements/choosing-numerals-or-words).

This means writing the words ‘zero’ and ‘one’ and using numerals for ‘2’ and above. The rules also say to use the numerals ‘0’ and ‘1’ in [specific situations](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/numbers-and-measurements/choosing-numerals-or-words#write_all_numbers_as_numerals_in_these_specific_situations).

For duration, the specific situations are likely to be when:

- you compare numbers in a sentence
- a sentence contains a series of numbers.

Write the words ‘zero’ and ‘one’ in sentences that don’t contain other numerals. Write the numerals ‘0’ and ‘1’ in sentences that contain numerals from 2 and above, or where all numbers show duration.

Spell out the units of time: ‘hours’, ‘minutes’ and ‘seconds’.
heading_path: Follow the manual’s number rules for duration
source.statement: Follow the manual's number rules for duration

source.body_excerpt:
It is usually better to spell out the units that measure time. This is particularly so in general content. Only use short forms if space is limited and the short forms are easy to identify correctly.

If you need to abbreviate time, use the following units as shortened forms:

- second – s
- minute – min
- hour – h
- day – d
- week – wk
- month – mo
- year – y or yr (Choose one and use it consistently in your document.)

The International System of Units – SI – is the international standard for measurement. The unit for second – symbol ‘s’ – is the [SI base unit for time](https://www.bipm.org/en/si-base-units/second).

Other time measures are not SI units – but ‘min’, ‘h’ and ‘d’ are used with ‘s’ and recognised as legal units of measurement in Australia. They are listed in Schedules 1 and 2 of the [National Measurement Regulations](https://www.legislation.gov.au/Details/F2019C00572).

There are also commonly-used shortened forms for time measures – for example, ‘wk’ (week), ‘mo’ (month) and ‘yr’ or ‘y’ (year). These are not legal units of time, but are likely to be understood when used alongside other time units.

If your expression contains one time measure only, insert a [non-br
heading_path: Use shortened forms for units of time when space is limited
source.statement: Use shortened forms for units of time when space is limited

violating_examples: 6hs
15mins
5d
3wks
8mo
2y or 2yr
But don’t space a number and its unit when your expression contains more than one time measure. Use a non-breaking space between each time value instead.
Never add an ‘s’ to show a plural.
11min12s
11 min 12 s
7hs 8mins 30s

Data systems support specific (and usually several) shortened forms for units of time. For example, hours might be: h, hh, hr, hours, hrs. They might also be case-sensitive or case-insensitive. You will need to check system specifications.

source.body_excerpt:
The prefix ‘bi’ can be confusing when used with expressions of time:

- ‘Bimonthly’ can mean either every 2 months or twice a month.
- ‘Biannual’ means twice a year.
- ‘Biennial’ means every 2 years.

Instead of using these words, be clear about the frequency and period of time you mean.
heading_path: Avoid using ‘bi’ to mean either 2 or twice
source.statement: Avoid using 'bi' to mean either 2 or twice

violating_examples: We meet biennially.

source.body_excerpt:
You can express a less-than-whole number as a decimal or as a fraction.

In text, write [decimal values as numerals](/node/198#write_all_numbers_as_numerals_in_these_specific_situations). Write [fractions as words](/node/198#use_words_for_2_and_above_in_these_specific_situations).
heading_path: Choose between a decimal value or fraction
source.statement: Choose between a decimal value or fraction

source.body_excerpt: Decimal values less than one have a ‘0’ before the decimal point.
heading_path: Use ‘0’ before a decimal point for values less than one
source.statement: Use '0' before a decimal point for values less than one

violating_examples: Always use a full stop, not a comma, for the decimal point. This is the style for Australian content.

compliant_examples: The square root of 56 is greater than the square root of 26.
We can prove that 0 does not equal 1.

source.body_excerpt:
In most content, explain mathematical relationships using words instead of symbols.

Many people will understand simple operations written with symbols (1 + 1 = 2). But other mathematical relationships are hard to understand unless they are written in words. Symbols might not be available in every font set and the default settings of screen readers might not read all symbols.

Remember that some users are unfamiliar with mathematical terminology. Make sure that you explain terms and concepts in plain language.

This rule applies to general content. If you’re writing specialist mathematical and scientific content, follow your publisher’s style.

In all mathematical expressions, [write numbers as numerals](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/numbers-and-measurements/choosing-numerals-or-words#write_all_numbers_as_numerals_in_these_specific_situations). This applies even when you use words to explain a relationship between the numbers.
heading_path: Use words instead of symbols to improve accessibility
source.statement: Use words instead of symbols to improve accessibility

violating_examples: We can prove that 0 ≠ 1.
We can prove that zero does not equal one.

source.body_excerpt:
Only use mathematical symbols in general content if user research shows they are appropriate for your users and for the type of content.

Complicated mathematical relationships are difficult to express in words and are best written using symbols. These are more likely to appear in technical content, but user research might show it is appropriate to reproduce them in general content.

If so, use the following guidance to write and space mathematical symbols correctly.
heading_path: Use symbols when user research supports their use
source.statement: Use symbols when user research supports their use

source.body_excerpt:
Always use the correct code for mathematical symbols, including:

- plus +
- minus −
- multiplication ×
- division ÷
- greater than >
- less than <
- greater than or equal to ≥
- less than or equal to ≤.

The +, −, ×, and ÷ symbols are called ‘operators’ because they carry out an operation on 2 elements of a mathematical expression. The >, <, ≥ and ≤ symbols are ‘relations’ because they show a relationship between 2 elements of a mathematical expression.

Don’t use punctuation marks (such as a dash) instead of a symbol.

Not all the symbols on your keyboard are coded correctly. It is better to insert a symbol using its Unicode character or Word’s Insert>Symbol command.

You will find other codes, such as HTML entities, in the table, ‘[Codes for mathematical symbols](#codes)’.
heading_path: Use symbols when user research supports their use
Use code, not punctuation, for mathematical symbols
source.statement: Use code, not punctuation, for mathematical symbols

source.body_excerpt:
The Style Manual uses ‘symbol’ rather than ‘sign’ when referring to particular mathematical symbols. For example, when writing about the symbol ‘+’, we use ‘plus symbol’ or ‘plus’ rather than ‘plus sign’.

In mathematics, the ‘sign’ of a number generally means whether it is positive or negative.

In non-technical writing however, it is acceptable to use the terms ‘plus sign’, ‘minus sign’, ‘multiplication sign’ and so on. ‘Sign’ is commonly used in general content to mean a mathematical symbol.
heading_path: Use symbols when user research supports their use
Note on terminology
source.statement: Note on terminology

source.body_excerpt:
Ratios don’t use a symbol, unlike mathematical operators. Ratios use a punctuation mark instead: the [colon](/node/104).

Ratios don’t have a space around the colon.
heading_path: Use symbols when user research supports their use
Don’t use a symbol or a space for ratios
source.statement: Don't use a symbol or a space for ratios

compliant_examples: The authors removed an outlier based on a Body Mass Index of less than 13 and greater than 97.
Only use petty cash for amounts less than $100.

source.body_excerpt:
When there is no space between a relation and a number, the expressions shows a range of numbers. For example, ‘<6.74’ refers to an infinitely large set of real numbers less than the number 6.74.

In most content, it is better to use words to avoid confusion: ‘less than 6.74’.
heading_path: Use symbols when user research supports their use
Don’t space >,<, ≥ and ≤ when they refer to a range of numbers
source.statement: Don't space >,<, ≥ and ≤ when they refer to a range of numbers

violating_examples: The authors removed an outlier based on a Body Mass Index of <13 and >97.
Only use petty cash for amounts <$100.

source.body_excerpt:
Insert a non-breaking space between numbers, letters and the symbol for an operator or a relation. A non-breaking space means that line breaks won’t separate a character from its symbol.

You can insert a non-breaking space using the Unicode character U+00A0.

In HTML, use the entity to insert a non-breaking space. You can also use the keyboard shortcut Ctrl+Shift+Spacebar in Word.
heading_path: Use a non-breaking space to keep characters and symbols together
source.statement: Use a non-breaking space to keep characters and symbols together

source.body_excerpt:
Symbols that modify a value rather than show an operation or a relationship, do not need a space.

Non-mathematical terms help to explain this.

When the symbol acts as a mathematical adjective, there is no space between the symbol and the character it modifies. An example is a positive or negative amount: +3 and −25.

When the symbol acts as a mathematical conjunction or verb, there are non-breaking spaces around the symbol. Examples are addition 6 + 6 = 12 and expressions that compare values such as 9 < 16. There are other examples in earlier sections on this page.

To avoid confusion in sentences, it is usually better to use words not symbols.
heading_path: Don’t use a space if a symbol modifies a value
source.statement: Don't use a space if a symbol modifies a value

violating_examples: The balance is −$10.

compliant_examples: x*×a*x*=b*x*a+[The index law of multiplication – no space between the variable and superscript exponent]b*x*=n*x*n-1+*x*n-2

source.body_excerpt:
An equation is a statement or question consisting of 2 mathematical expressions linked by an equals symbol (=).

Use equations if user research supports their inclusion.

The Unicode character for the equals symbol is U+003D.

Put a [non-breaking space](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/numbers-and-measurements/mathematical-relationships#use_a_nonbreaking_space_to_keep_characters_and_symbols_together) around the equals symbol and around all operators except for the division slash – it is unspaced. If you think the equation is clearer with a space around the division slash, use a narrow no-break space (U+202F) or thin space (U+2009).

There is no space between a character and its superscript or subscript.
heading_path: Use the correct style for equations
source.statement: Use the correct style for equations

violating_examples: x*×a*x*=b*x*a+[Variable and superscripts are spaced]b*x*=n*x*n-1+*x*n-2

source.body_excerpt:
An equation can be set ‘inline’ within a line of text or ‘displayed’ on a line of its own.

Displayed equations are indented, centred or left-aligned.

For general content, the Style Manual recommends using a displayed equation set as a block quotation. Code the block quotation with the HTML <blockquote> element.

Don’t introduce the equation with a colon, but do use other sentence punctuation. For example, if the equation ends a sentence, follow the equation with a full stop.>
heading_path: Use the correct style for equations
Set equations as block quotations
source.statement: Set equations as block quotations

source.body_excerpt:
Australia uses the metric system for most quantities:

- The modern form of the metric system is the
[International System of Units](https://www.bipm.org/en/measurement-units/ )(SI). - Australia also uses some non-SI legal units of measurement, which are listed in
[Schedules 1 and 2 of the National Measurement Regulations](https://www.legislation.gov.au/Details/F2012C00400).

The National Measurement Institute oversees [Australian units of measurement](https://www.industry.gov.au/regulations-and-standards/australias-measurement-system). The governing legislation is the [ National Measurement Act 1960](https://www.legislation.gov.au/Series/C1960A00064).

Don’t use the non-SI legal units of measurement for international content. The exception is when you have checked that ~~ ~~users will understand and accept them.

Rules for units of measurement:

- Punctuation: don’t place a full stop after a unit of measurement.
- Capitalisation: use capitals only if the unit represents a proper name.
- Plural and possessive: units don’t have a plural or possessive form.
- Start of a sentence: write out the unit in full.
- Spacing: use a non-breaking space between the number and the unit.
heading_path: Use the standard units of measurement
source.statement: Use the standard units of measurement

source.body_excerpt:
Use numerals, not words, for numbers when you are referring to a unit of measurement:

- Always use numerals next to a unit of measurement.
- Include a non-breaking space between the number and the unit.
heading_path: Write numerals with units of measurement
source.statement: Write numerals with units of measurement

violating_examples: five t
five tonnes

source.body_excerpt: You don’t need to spell out units of measurement, even for the first use, if they’re well known and users will know what they mean.
heading_path: Use symbols for common units of measurement
source.statement: Use symbols for common units of measurement

violating_examples: Queensland is 1,853 million square km in area.

source.body_excerpt:
People will read the number and its unit as a measurement only if the 2 components sit together. To do this, use a non-breaking space between numbers and their units of measurement.

Without a non-breaking space, a unit could reflow to the next line. This would separate it from the quantity, making it difficult for users to understand the information being presented.

Although this is important for all content, it’s more likely to happen on smaller screens, such as those on mobile devices.
heading_path: Put a non-breaking space between numbers and units
source.statement: Put a non-breaking space between numbers and units

violating_examples: The post should be at least 1.5
m tall.
By convention, some industries don’t have a space between the quantity and the unit. Many 750 mL bottles of wine, for example, have the volume 750mL printed on the label.
Check the preferred style if you are writing for a specialist application.

source.body_excerpt: Symbols for units of measurement represent both the singular and the plural forms. Don’t use an ‘s’ to show plural with the symbols for units.
heading_path: Don’t add ‘s’ for plural forms
source.statement: Don't add 's' for plural forms

violating_examples: 56 kms

source.body_excerpt:
Don’t use imperial units of measurement in Australia unless you have a specific reason, such as:

- in quotations from historical documents
- when writing for readers in countries (particularly the United States) where imperial measures, or elements of them, still apply.
heading_path: Avoid imperial units
source.statement: Avoid imperial units

source.body_excerpt:
Spell out ordinal numbers from ‘first’ to ‘ninth’. Use numerals for ordinals from ‘10th’ onwards.

Ordinals written as numerals always have a suffix:

- ‘-st’ (‘first’, ‘21st’)
- ‘-nd’ (‘second’, ‘32nd’)
- ‘-rd’ (‘third’, ‘103rd’)
- ‘-th’ (‘fourth’, ‘15th’, ‘55th’ and so on).

Don’t write suffixes in superscript. Superscript may not be accessible to people who use screen readers.
heading_path: Use words for ordinals up to ‘ninth’ and numerals for ‘10th’ and above
source.statement: Use words for ordinals up to 'ninth' and numerals for '10th' and above

source.body_excerpt:
Don’t use ordinals to order points in general content. Reword the content so it doesn’t need ordinals or use a numbered list instead. A list can make it easier for people to follow the sequence.

Always use numbered lists rather than ordinals when you’re expressing a series of items or steps – for example, in recommendations or instructions.
heading_path: Create a list rather than use ordinals
source.statement: Create a list rather than use ordinals

violating_examples: If you want to apply for the grant, first complete the eligibility checklist. Second, you must submit a business case; and third, you must provide supporting documents.

source.body_excerpt: Use numerals without a suffix for dates.
heading_path: Don't use ordinals in dates
source.statement: Don't use ordinals in dates

violating_examples: 12th February 2020

source.body_excerpt:
Regnal numbers are upper case roman numerals that are used for the titles of monarchs and popes and in family names.

Even though you might pronounce regnals as ordinal numbers, don’t write them like that.
heading_path: Don’t confuse ordinals with regnal numbers
source.statement: Don't confuse ordinals with regnal numbers

violating_examples: Elizabeth Ist

source.body_excerpt:
Put a non-breaking space between the name and the regnal number. A non-breaking space means that line breaks won’t split up both elements of the name. The name and number will stay together on one line.

You can insert a non-breaking space using the Unicode character U+00A0.

In HTML, use the entity to insert a non-breaking space. You can also use the keyboard shortcut Ctrl+Shift+Spacebar in Word.
heading_path: Don’t confuse ordinals with regnal numbers
Use a non-breaking space for names with regnal numbers
source.statement: Use a non-breaking space for names with regnal numbers

compliant_examples: Fifty-five per cent of the council’s revenue came from rates.
The price of Tapis oil is up by 0.25%.

source.body_excerpt: Use the percentage sign next to a numeral in text. Don’t use a space between the number and the percentage sign.
heading_path: Use numerals with the percentage sign
source.statement: Use numerals with the percentage sign

violating_examples: 55% of the council’s revenue came from rates.
Use decimals rather than fractions with the percentage sign.
The price of Tapis oil is up by 1/4%.
As for any number, avoid starting a sentence with the percentage. Reword the sentence if possible, or write the percentage out in words. You can use everyday words if a precise amount is not needed.

compliant_examples: Statistics show the percentage of Australians with university degrees is increasing.

source.body_excerpt: ‘Per cent’ and ‘percentage’ aren’t the same. The term ‘per cent’ is an adverb. The noun form is ‘percentage’.
heading_path: Use the correct form of the noun (percentage)
source.statement: Use the correct form of the noun (percentage)

violating_examples: Statistics show the per cent of Australians with university degrees is increasing.
‘Per cent’ is written as 2 words in Australia. ‘Percent’ is not Australian spelling.

source.body_excerpt:
Avoid using percentages to describe changes.

Tell people what the actual increase or decrease is.
heading_path: Don’t use percentages to describe change
source.statement: Don't use percentages to describe change

violating_examples: The application fee increased by 40% from $50 to $70 on 1 January 2020.

source.body_excerpt: When you use many percentages in body text, put the figures in brackets (parentheses) or use a list to simplify the text.
heading_path: Be concise when writing about percentages
source.statement: Be concise when writing about percentages

violating_examples: In 2019, the largest sources of population growth were New South Wales, Queensland and Victoria. New South Wales accounted for 32% of the population growth, Queensland 20%, and Victoria 19%.

source.body_excerpt:
Break telephone numbers into shorter blocks of digits or ‘chunks’.

Telephone numbers are easier to read when their digits are chunked, rather than written in one large group.

Australian telephone numbers in general use have no more than 10 digits:

- Landlines – 2 digits for the area code followed by 8 digits for the rest of the telephone number.
- Mobiles – 10 digits (there is no area code).

There are also categories of telephone numbers that don’t have 10 digits – for example, ‘13’ numbers have 6 digits.
heading_path: Use ‘chunks’ of digits to help people read telephone numbers
source.statement: Use 'chunks' of digits to help people read telephone numbers

source.body_excerpt:
Use a non-breaking space between chunks of digits in a telephone number. A non-breaking space means that line breaks won’t split up the number. The telephone number will stay together on one line.

You can insert a non-breaking space using the Unicode character U+00A0.

In HTML, use the entity to insert a non-breaking space. You can also use the keyboard shortcut Ctrl+Shift+Spacebar in Word.
heading_path: Put a non-breaking space between the chunks of digits
source.statement: Put a non-breaking space between the chunks of digits

source.body_excerpt: Write telephone numbers in a format appropriate for the location of the users.
heading_path: Write telephone numbers in the national or international format
source.statement: Write telephone numbers in the national or international format

source.body_excerpt:
‘Click-to-call’ allows users to call a telephone number by selecting (clicking) the number shown in content. When the user selects the number, the user’s mobile phone, other mobile device or personal computer (if it has a supporting application) calls the number.

Click-to-call makes telephone numbers more accessible because users don’t need to copy the number manually. Click-to-call also works with screen readers.

Devices sometimes recognise when a number in content is a telephone number and automatically treat the number as a click-to-call link. This is not always the case, so use HTML code to support this functionality. Seek specialist advice if you’re unsure of how to do this.
heading_path: Make telephone numbers accessible through ‘click-to-call’ functionality
source.statement: Make telephone numbers accessible through 'click-to-call' functionality

source.body_excerpt:
Always display the telephone number as digits. Don’t use ‘phone words’. Use the relevant 13 or 1300 number instead.

Some organisations use phone words to advertise their telephone number as a digit-word combination. Don’t do this, because some people find it hard to convert letters to numbers.
heading_path: Don't use ‘phone words’
source.statement: Don't use 'phone words'

violating_examples: 13 VETS

source.body_excerpt:
Every sentence has at least one main clause. The main clause is also known as:

- a principal clause
- an independent clause.

The main clause has at least one complete (finite) verb and can stand alone as a sentence.
heading_path: A main clause can stand alone as a sentence
source.statement: A main clause can stand alone as a sentence

heading_path: Follow the possession rules for different types of nouns
source.statement: Follow the possession rules for different types of nouns

source.body_excerpt:
There are 4 types of shortened forms: [abbreviations](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/format-writing-and-structure/clear-language-and-writing-style/plain-language-and-word-choice/abbreviations), [contractions](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/format-writing-and-structure/clear-language-and-writing-style/plain-language-and-word-choice/contractions), [acronyms and initialisms](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/format-writing-and-structure/clear-language-and-writing-style/plain-language-and-word-choice/acronyms-and-initialisms).

Only use shortened forms if users will understand them. Make sure they are appropriate for your content’s context, purpose and tone.

Add an apostrophe and ‘s’ to show possession for [shortened forms](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/shortened-words-and-phrases).
heading_path: Add an apostrophe and ‘s’ to form a possessive shortened form
source.statement: Add an apostrophe and 's' to form a possessive shortened form

source.body_excerpt: Add an ‘s’ to form the plural of shortened forms such as [acronyms and initialisms](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/format-writing-and-structure/clear-language-and-writing-style/plain-language-and-word-choice/acronyms-and-initialisms). Don’t write an apostrophe before the ‘s’. The same rule applies when [making nouns plural](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/types-words/nouns#nouns_can_be_singular_or_plural).
heading_path: Add an apostrophe and ‘s’ to form a possessive shortened form
Add ‘s’ to make a plural shortened form – not apostrophe and ‘s’
source.statement: Add 's' to make a plural shortened form – not apostrophe and 's'

violating_examples: MP’s
LGA’s
PC’s
Add an apostrophe to plural shortened forms to show possession.

compliant_examples: The Department of Veterans’ Affairs (DVA) has information about veteran support officers on its website. DVA supports …
Use the Moneysmart savings goal calculator from the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC). ASIC created Moneysmart to …

source.body_excerpt:
Define a shortened form the first time you use it (unless you’re certain users will understand it without a definition). Follow the spelt-out term with its shortened form in parentheses.

Avoid using a possessive apostrophe when you do this. It can be difficult to decide where to put the apostrophe and the sentence is often harder to read.

Use the shortened form rather than the full term if you mention the term again.
heading_path: Add an apostrophe and ‘s’ to form a possessive shortened form
Don’t use a possessive when defining a shortened form
source.statement: Don't use a possessive when defining a shortened form

violating_examples: Find information about veteran support officers on the Department of Veterans’ Affairs’ (DVA’s) website. DVA supports …
Use the Australian Securities and Investments Commission’s (ASIC’s) Moneysmart savings goal calculator. ASIC created Moneysmart to …

source.body_excerpt: Don’t use an apostrophe for [Australian place names](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/node/134) involving possessives.
heading_path: Don’t use an apostrophe for an Australian place name
source.statement: Don't use an apostrophe for an Australian place name

source.body_excerpt:
Noun phrases about plural time periods don’t need apostrophes because they’re usually descriptive, not possessive.

In phrases such as ‘6 months retired’ or ‘5 months pregnant’, the time periods are clearly adjectival. They don’t show possession.

Other noun phrases aren’t possessive because they are conversational shorthand for an ‘of’ phrase. For example, ‘in 4 days time’ is shorthand for ‘in 4 days of time’.

Some styles use an apostrophe to stand for the word ‘of’ and don't use it for descriptive phrases. For many years, the Style Manual has recommended the simple rule of no apostrophe for either use.
heading_path: Don’t use an apostrophe for a period of time
source.statement: Don't use an apostrophe for a period of time

source.body_excerpt: No apostrophe is needed for the [plural form of a noun](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/types-words/nouns#nouns_can_be_singular_or_plural). This type of error is known as the ‘greengrocer’s apostrophe’.
heading_path: Don’t use an apostrophe to make a noun plural
source.statement: Don't use an apostrophe to make a noun plural

violating_examples: the 2020’s
committee report’s
newer 747’s
fresh avocado’s

source.body_excerpt:
Apostrophes show sounds in words from other languages.

This occurs when words in certain languages are ‘transliterated’, that is, when words in other languages are written using letters of the English alphabet.

In our examples, the apostrophe is a transliteration of a letter with a diacritic mark that represents the sound of a glottal stop.

If you’re unsure whether an apostrophe is needed, consult your dictionary for the preferred spelling.
heading_path: An apostrophe can stand in for a sound
source.statement: An apostrophe can stand in for a sound

source.body_excerpt:
Brackets can help you break up information. They enclose parts of the sentence that aren’t essential to the meaning. Sentences must be grammatically correct if you remove the text in brackets.

The most commonly used brackets are:

- parentheses
- square brackets.

Use brackets sparingly for:

- non-essential information
[shortened forms](/node/92)- references
- insertions.

Use brackets only where they make content clearer to people. For example, always use brackets in [author–date citations](/node/165#examples_of_authordate_citations).

Too many brackets, or badly used brackets, can make a sentence more complex and difficult to understand. You can usually rewrite a sentence so the content in brackets can be its own sentence or can even be removed.

Other types of brackets, such as curly brackets and slant brackets, are used in fields such as mathematics and linguistics. These are specialist uses, so don’t use them in most content.
heading_path: Use brackets for text users can skip over
source.statement: Use brackets for text users can skip over

source.body_excerpt:
Information in parentheses is less important than information that is between [spaced en dashes](/node/199) or pairs of [commas](/node/109).

Used well, parentheses can improve meaning and make content easy to scan.
heading_path: Put extra information in parentheses
source.statement: Put extra information in parentheses

source.body_excerpt: Reword the text to avoid square brackets inside of parentheses wherever possible.
heading_path: Avoid using square brackets in parentheses
source.statement: Avoid using square brackets in parentheses

violating_examples: Australia’s Parliament House (architects Mitchell/Giurgola & Thorp (New York)) opened on 9 May 1988.

source.body_excerpt:
Use square brackets in [quoted material](/node/114) to show that you have:

- paraphrased the original content
- inserted text that was not in the original content.
heading_path: Use square brackets to show insertions in quotes
source.statement: Use square brackets to show insertions in quotes

compliant_examples: The winning tenderer (a local company) signed the contract on Tuesday.
The winning tenderer signed the contract on Tuesday. They were a local company.
The winning tenderer (a local company) signed the contract on Tuesday.

source.body_excerpt: Punctuation in brackets depends on what is inside the brackets. Punctuate content in brackets as you would if it were outside the brackets.
heading_path: Follow normal punctuation rules for content in brackets
source.statement: Follow normal punctuation rules for content in brackets

violating_examples: The winning tenderer (a local company), signed the contract on Tuesday.
If the content inside the brackets is a full sentence, include the end punctuation inside the brackets.
The winning tenderer (They were a local company.) signed the contract on Tuesday.

compliant_examples: The most recent review of defence policy (*2016 Defence white paper*) set the direction for the next 10 years.

source.body_excerpt:
Brackets should be in the same type (roman, italics, bold) as the text around the brackets. This is regardless of the type of the text inside the brackets.

This is the same rule as for [quotation marks](/node/114).
heading_path: Write brackets in the same type as the surrounding text
source.statement: Write brackets in the same type as the surrounding text

violating_examples: The most recent review of defence policy *(2016 Defence white paper)* set the direction for the next 10 years.

source.body_excerpt: Use a colon only if you are sure it is needed. Incorrect use creates confusion for users.
heading_path: Limit colon use
source.statement: Limit colon use

source.body_excerpt:
Use a colon to:

- introduce a word, phrase or clause that provides more detail
- introduce a question
- give an example
- summarise or contrast with what comes before it.
heading_path: Introduce examples and contrasts with colons
source.statement: Introduce examples and contrasts with colons

compliant_examples: Pick any 2 of low price, high speed and high quality.
The requirements for the position are strong communication skills and experience across content management platforms.

source.body_excerpt: Use a colon to introduce a list of words, phrases or clauses.
heading_path: Start lists with a colon
source.statement: Start lists with a colon

violating_examples: Pick any 2 of: low price, high speed and high quality.
The requirements for the position are: strong communication skills and experience across content management platforms.
Include the colon to restructure content into bulleted lists.

compliant_examples: We had to write 66 reports: it took months.
The commander was confident: Special Air Service Regiment had enough ammunition.

source.body_excerpt:
Start the word after the colon with a lower case letter unless:

- the word that follows the colon is a
[proper noun](/node/122#proper_nouns_are_the_names_of_specific_things) - the text after the colon is a question that is a complete sentence.
heading_path: Use lower case following a colon in most cases
source.statement: Use lower case following a colon in most cases

violating_examples: The election was fought on a simple question: which party had the best economic credentials?
If the colon introduces a series of sentences or questions, use a lead-in and colon to introduce them in a bulleted or numbered list.
We had to write many reports: It took months.
The commander was confident: special air service regiment had enough ammunition.
After a colon, capitalise the first word of questions that are complete sentences. This makes it clear that the question mark applies only to the text after the colon.

source.body_excerpt: Use a colon before the subtitle of a book or article. Follow the colon with a lower case letter, unless it’s a proper noun.
heading_path: Start subtitles of books and articles with a colon
source.statement: Start subtitles of books and articles with a colon

source.body_excerpt: Use a colon to introduce a block quotation. Block quotations should also be coded with the HTML <blockquote> element.
heading_path: Introduce block quotations with colons
source.statement: Introduce block quotations with colons

source.body_excerpt: Use a colon to give a [mathematical ratio](/node/145). Don’t put a space after the colon.
heading_path: Write mathematical ratios with a colon
source.statement: Write mathematical ratios with a colon

source.body_excerpt:
A comma separates introductory words, phrases and clauses from the main clause of the sentence.

Many introductory phrases can be moved to the end of sentences without changing the meaning. In these cases, you don’t need a comma before the phrase. This simpler structure can be easier to read.
heading_path: Separate introductory words, phrases and clauses with a comma
source.statement: Separate introductory words, phrases and clauses with a comma

source.body_excerpt: Use a comma after introductory words, such as greetings and adverbs, or when addressing someone. Using an introductory word gives it emphasis.
heading_path: Separate introductory words, phrases and clauses with a comma
Place a comma after adverbs and other introductory words
source.statement: Place a comma after adverbs and other introductory words

source.body_excerpt: Use commas after [adverbial phrases](/node/127) and [adverbial clauses](/node/127). Adverbs – such as ‘first’ and ‘during’ – modify verbs, adjectives and other adverbs.
heading_path: Separate introductory words, phrases and clauses with a comma
Use a comma after phrases and clauses that change the whole sentence
source.statement: Use a comma after phrases and clauses that change the whole sentence

compliant_examples: There were 16.5 million people enrolled to vote in Australian elections on 18 April 2019.

source.body_excerpt:
Use a comma after an introductory phrase that ends with a numeral and is immediately followed by another numeral. It doesn’t matter how short the sentence is.

Avoid this type of sentence structure because the string of numbers can be confusing.
heading_path: Separate introductory words, phrases and clauses with a comma
Avoid beginning a sentence with a string of numbers and dates
source.statement: Avoid beginning a sentence with a string of numbers and dates

violating_examples: On 18 April 2019, 16.5 million people were enrolled to vote in Australian elections.

source.body_excerpt:
Commas isolate information in a sentence when it isn’t essential to:

- meaning
- grammatical structure.

Within a sentence, use a pair of commas to separate non-essential or supplementary information. Always check for the second comma where there should be a pair.

Generally, if you can take out part of the sentence and it is still grammatically correct, it should be between a pair of commas.

Check carefully. Using comma pairs can completely change the meaning of a sentence.
heading_path: Mark out non‐essential information within a sentence
source.statement: Mark out non-essential information within a sentence

compliant_examples: The report was tabled last week. It is about demographic changes in rural areas in Western Australia.

source.body_excerpt:
Use commas around clauses that add information but aren’t essential to the meaning of the sentence.

Don’t use commas if the clause is essential for meaning.

If you can remove the clause and your sentence means the same thing, it’s non-essential and should go between commas.

Non-essential clauses are also called ‘non-restrictive’ or ‘non-defining’ [clauses](/node/143).
heading_path: Mark out non‐essential information within a sentence
Set off non-essential clauses
source.statement: Set off non-essential clauses

violating_examples: The report, detailing demographic changes in rural areas in Western Australia, was tabled last week.

compliant_examples: The strike took place in Whyalla, South Australia, in June 2014.

source.body_excerpt: Use a pair of commas when you have 2 noun phrases next to each other that define the same thing.
heading_path: Mark out non‐essential information within a sentence
Place commas around nouns that define the same thing they follow
source.statement: Place commas around nouns that define the same thing they follow

violating_examples: The strike took place in Whyalla, South Australia in June 2014.
You should be able to take out the noun phrase between the comma pair and still have a grammatically correct sentence.

source.body_excerpt: Questions can be tagged onto the end of sentences. Use a comma before a question that is part of the sentence.
heading_path: Mark out non‐essential information within a sentence
Separate questions tagged onto a sentence
source.statement: Separate questions tagged onto a sentence

source.body_excerpt: Generally, use a comma before and after the phrase ‘for example’ in a sentence.
heading_path: Mark out non‐essential information within a sentence
Use commas with the phrase ‘for example’
source.statement: Use commas with the phrase 'for example'

compliant_examples: Exports of rare earths (e.g. lithium, europium) have soared.

source.body_excerpt: If you use [Latin shortened forms](/node/91), such as ‘e.g.’ and ‘i.e.’, don’t follow them with a comma.
heading_path: Mark out non‐essential information within a sentence
Don’t use commas with Latin shortened forms
source.statement: Don't use commas with Latin shortened forms

violating_examples: Exports of rare earths (e.g., lithium and europium) have soared.

source.body_excerpt:
Use commas to connect 2 or more [principal clauses](/node/143#a_principal_clause_can_stand_alone_as_a_sentence) joined by a [coordinating conjunction](/node/129#coordinating_conjunctions_join_things_of_equal_importance) (‘and’, ‘or’, ‘but’, ‘so’).

If they have different subjects, use a comma before the coordinating conjunction.

Do not use this rule to create a sentence of more than 25 words. Shorter sentences are easier to read.
heading_path: Place commas between principal clauses joined together with a conjunction
source.statement: Place commas between principal clauses joined together with a conjunction

compliant_examples: The report was finished last week, but the minister has not approved its release.

source.body_excerpt: Don’t use a comma to link 2 stand-alone sentences unless you use a coordinating conjunction. This kind of error is called a ‘comma splice’.
heading_path: Place commas between principal clauses joined together with a conjunction
Don’t use commas to ‘splice’ sentences
source.statement: Don't use commas to 'splice' sentences

violating_examples: The report was finished last week, the minister has not approved its release.

heading_path: Punctuate sentence lists and strings of adjectives
source.statement: Punctuate sentence lists and strings of adjectives

source.body_excerpt:
Use commas between items in a sentence list. Avoid using a comma before the last item in the list.

This rule applies to sentence lists and sentence fragments in bullet lists. Do not punctuate the end of a list item with a comma if it is in a bullet list.
heading_path: Punctuate sentence lists and strings of adjectives
Separate items in lists of nouns or adjectives with commas
source.statement: Separate items in lists of nouns or adjectives with commas

source.body_excerpt:
