When writing strings of adjectives, use a set order – [evaluative, descriptive, then definitive](/node/126#strings_of_adjectives_have_a_naturalsounding_order).

Use commas in strings of adjectives of the same type (for example, a string of descriptive adjectives).
heading_path: Punctuate sentence lists and strings of adjectives
Separate adjectives of the same type
source.statement: Separate adjectives of the same type

compliant_examples: The agency handles around 6,500 complaints each year.

source.body_excerpt:
Numbers with 4 or more digits (starting from 1,000) need a comma. Use commas for numerals in text and in tables.

Don’t use a space between the digits, because screen readers can read them as separate numbers.
heading_path: Use commas in numbers with 4 or more digits
source.statement: Use commas in numbers with 4 or more digits

violating_examples: The agency handles around 6 500 complaints each year.
When you are using numbers of 1,000 or more, use commas to separate the numerals into groups of 3 (working right to left).

source.body_excerpt:
Numbers below a million are usually easy to read as numerals. Use a combination of words and numerals for [large, rounded numbers from a million](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/numbers-and-measurements/choosing-numerals-or-words#combine_numerals_and_words_for_large_rounded_numbers).

Large, rounded numbers are punctuated with a [decimal point](/node/146).
heading_path: Use commas in numbers with 4 or more digits
Use numerals and words for large, rounded numbers
source.statement: Use numerals and words for large, rounded numbers

source.body_excerpt: Introduce directly quoted speech with a comma. Use the comma in combination with quotation marks.
heading_path: Show direct speech or quoted material using commas
source.statement: Show direct speech or quoted material using commas

source.body_excerpt:
En dashes are half the width of the font height. Use them as a type of punctuation.

Don’t use an en dash instead of a minus symbol. Screen readers will read dashes as dashes, not as the minus symbol.

In Unicode, the en dash is U+2013. Use the entity – in HTML.

To make sure screen readers read the minus symbol, use the mathematical symbol for minus. In Unicode, this is U+2212. Use the entity − in HTML.

Don’t confuse the dash or the minus symbol for a [hyphen](/node/105).
heading_path: Use the correct symbols for en dash and minus symbol
source.statement: Use the correct symbols for en dash and minus symbol

source.body_excerpt:
En dashes show a span when used with numerals, such as in a financial year, a range of values or span of time. En dashes sometimes appear in a span of words, such as in a span of days of the week.

Avoid using en dashes in most content.

Dashes can affect readability unless a user changes their screen reader’s default settings (punctuation verbosity settings). Screen readers generally won’t read out dashes by default. This can affect people’s ability to quickly understand spans.

That is why, in general content, it’s better to use phrases for most spans of numbers. You can use en dashes in technical content, particularly if it contains a lot of spans.
heading_path: Use a phrase instead of an en dash for most spans of numbers
source.statement: Use a phrase instead of an en dash for most spans of numbers

source.body_excerpt:
There are exceptions to the rule of using phrases for spans in general content. The exceptions are for particular date spans and time spans.

Use en dashes for date spans in:

- financial years
- calendar years
- the titles of publications and programs
- terms of office
- lifespans (birth and death)
- limited space.

Date spans in headings should follow the general rule, except when:

- the heading contains a title that has an en dash
- using words would push the character count over 70 characters (including spaces).

Only use en dashes for time spans when you have limited space.
heading_path: Follow exceptions to the general rule
source.statement: Follow exceptions to the general rule

source.body_excerpt:
For financial years, use 4 digits for the first number and only 2 digits for the second. Join them with an unspaced en dash.

Use the phrases ‘financial year’ and ‘financial years’ at first mention, unless the context makes the meaning clear.
heading_path: Follow exceptions to the general rule
Use an en dash for a financial year
source.statement: Use an en dash for a financial year

source.body_excerpt:
For calendar years, use 4 digits for the first number and either 4 or 2 digits for the second number. Join them with an unspaced en dash.

Use the phrases ‘calendar year’ and ‘calendar years’ at first mention, unless the context makes the meaning clear.
heading_path: Follow exceptions to the general rule
Use an en dash for a calendar year
source.statement: Use an en dash for a calendar year

source.body_excerpt:
Date spans often appear in the titles of government publications and programs. When you create a title, use 4 digits for the first year and 2 digits for the second year. If you cross the century, always use 4 digits for both years.

Use 4 digits on both sides of the span for these titles if that is your organisation’s house style.

When you refer to a title published by another person or organisation, retain the style that was originally used for year spans.
heading_path: Follow exceptions to the general rule
Use an en dash for a date span in titles of publications and programs
source.statement: Use an en dash for a date span in titles of publications and programs

source.body_excerpt: A person’s term of office usually appears in parentheses after the person’s name. Always use 4 digits for both dates, joined by an unspaced en dash.
heading_path: Follow exceptions to the general rule
Use an en dash for a term of office
source.statement: Use an en dash for a term of office

violating_examples: Australia’s prime minister at the start of the Depression was James Scullin (1929–32).

source.body_excerpt: Dates of birth and death usually appear in parentheses after the person’s name. Always use 4 digits for both dates, joined by an unspaced en dash.
heading_path: Follow exceptions to the general rule
Use an en dash for a person’s lifespan
source.statement: Use an en dash for a person's lifespan

violating_examples: Caroline Chisholm (1808–77)

source.body_excerpt:
Using en dashes for date spans is allowed when you have limited space. This could be in display text, tables, lists or in social media posts.

Use the following style for en dashes in spans of days and months:

- The en dash is spaced when the day and month appear on both sides of the span.
- The en dash is unspaced when the month only appears at the end of the span.
heading_path: Follow exceptions to the general rule
Use an en dash for a date span when space is limited
source.statement: Use an en dash for a date span when space is limited

source.body_excerpt:
In technical content where there are many numbers, you can use en dashes for number, date and page spans. Don’t combine en dashes with ‘from’ or ‘to’ in the spans.

The en dash is unspaced when it connects only 2 numbers.
heading_path: Use an en dash for spans in technical content
source.statement: Use an en dash for spans in technical content

source.body_excerpt:
A hyphen normally attaches a prefix to an adjectival phrase. In some cases, an en dash is correct, not a hyphen.

If the phrase is not hyphenated, such as in a proper adjectival phrase, you can use an en dash between the prefix and the first word.

The capitalisation of the proper adjectival phrase and the en dash show that the prefix applies to all the words.
heading_path: Rewrite to avoid joining a prefix with an en dash
source.statement: Rewrite to avoid joining a prefix with an en dash

source.body_excerpt:
To show a sudden interruption in quotations and reported speech, use 2 em dashes in a row. The 2 em dashes follow a space.

Ellipses cannot be used for this purpose, as they show the writer has deliberately left out quoted speech. Read related guidance on [ellipses](/node/115).
heading_path: Use 2 em dashes for some quoted speech and deliberate omissions in text
source.statement: Use 2 em dashes for some quoted speech and deliberate omissions in text

source.body_excerpt:
The ellipsis (plural ‘ellipses’) is a character of exactly 3 dots.

Use the ellipsis:

- if you omit words in quoted text
- to mark an unfinished
[phrase, clause or sentence](/node/120).
heading_path: Show missing words or ideas with ellipses
source.statement: Show missing words or ideas with ellipses

source.body_excerpt:
Use the symbol for the ellipsis. Don’t use a string of full stops. Insert it using:

- the unicode character U+2026
- the HTML code <…>
- in many software applications, Alt+Ctrl+. or Option;.
heading_path: Do not use a string of full stops
source.statement: Do not use a string of full stops

compliant_examples: The evaluation concluded, ‘The report is well written, but it needs … more work.’
The evaluation concluded, ‘The report is well written, but …’

source.body_excerpt: Use a single space before and after each ellipsis.
heading_path: Add spaces around ellipses
source.statement: Add spaces around ellipses

violating_examples: The evaluation concluded, ‘The report is well written, but it needs…more work.’
The evaluation concluded, ‘The report is well written, but…’

The exception to this rule is if the quote ends in an exclamation mark or question mark. Include the final punctuation mark after the ellipsis. Don’t include a space between the punctuation and the ellipsis.

compliant_examples: The report is well written, but it needs rewriting now circumstances have changed … There is now an obvious need for more work.

source.body_excerpt: Use ellipses sparingly. Overusing ellipses can lead to a suspicion that you are misquoting. Don’t leave out important details or change the original intent of the quoted material.
heading_path: Don’t change the original intent of quoted material
source.statement: Don't change the original intent of quoted material

violating_examples: The report … needs rewriting … obvious need for more work.

source.body_excerpt:
Exclamation marks aren’t part of [government voice](/node/40). Don’t use exclamation marks in formal content, such as government reports or briefings.

In general use, exclamation marks can emphasise:

- statements
- emotions
- greetings
- commands
- rhetorical questions.
heading_path: Don’t use exclamation marks in general
source.statement: Don't use exclamation marks in general

violating_examples: A state of emergency has been declared for all areas of the ACT!
Exclamation marks often appear ‘as themselves’ in instructions to users of government services.

compliant_examples: Were you born overseas or have a parent who was? Nearly half of Australians do!

source.body_excerpt:
Don’t use exclamation marks too often. Exclamation marks can lose their emphasis if you use too many.

At the end of each sentence you want to emphasise, use only one exclamation mark.
heading_path: Write one exclamation mark: don’t overuse them
source.statement: Write one exclamation mark: don't overuse them

violating_examples: Were you born overseas or have a parent who was? Nearly half of Australians do!!!
Some people use multiple exclamation marks in social media. This is not suitable for government content.

source.body_excerpt:
The forward slash is also known as the ‘solidus’ or just the ‘slash’.

Use forward slashes:

- in some shortened forms
- in mathematical expressions
- to present lines of poetry in body text
- instead of ‘per’, ‘an’ or ‘a’ when abbreviating units of measurement
- in web addresses
- in dates if you can’t write them out – for example, in tables
- in some place names.
heading_path: Limit the forward slash to specific uses
source.statement: Limit the forward slash to specific uses

source.body_excerpt:
There is no need to include a space on either side of a forward slash.

The exceptions are for:

[official dual place names](/node/134#check_official_place_names_and_style_them_correctly)- lines of poetry in body text – use forward slashes with spaces around them to show the line breaks.
heading_path: Don’t add spaces around most forward slashes
source.statement: Don't add spaces around most forward slashes

source.body_excerpt: Don’t use forward slashes when spelling out [units of measurement](/node/147).
heading_path: Write shortened units of measurement with a forward slash
source.statement: Write shortened units of measurement with a forward slash

violating_examples: 60 kilometres/hour

source.body_excerpt: Don’t use a forward slash as a replacement for an en dash in financial years.
heading_path: Use an en dash for financial years, not a slash
source.statement: Use an en dash for financial years, not a slash

source.body_excerpt: When showing alternatives, use ‘or’ instead of a forward slash. This is easier for people to understand.
heading_path: Write ‘or’ instead of a slash for alternatives
source.statement: Write 'or' instead of a slash for alternatives

violating_examples: a yes/no question
Do not use ‘and/or’* *in text. It could mean either ‘and’ or ‘or’, which confuses many users. Rewrite the sentence to make the meaning clear.

source.body_excerpt: Don’t use a forward slash between words that retain their separate identities. Instead, either use an en dash or reword the sentence. Forward slashes can make it look like you mean to show an alternative.
heading_path: Don’t join words with a slash
source.statement: Don't join words with a slash

violating_examples: a Sydney/Brisbane flight

source.body_excerpt:
Also use full stops:

- as the decimal point in numbers and currency – for example, ‘$3.55’
- in numbering subsections and paragraphs in a document – for example, ‘Section 7.3’
- in some
[Latin shortened forms](/node/91)and[shortened forms used in referencing](/node/92).

Don’t use full stops with [contractions](/node/191) or most [abbreviations](/node/184).
heading_path: Use full stops with some numbers and shortened forms
source.statement: Use full stops with some numbers and shortened forms

source.body_excerpt: Do not use a full stop after a web or email address if it’s part of a sentence fragment or on a line by itself.
heading_path: Don’t end web or email addresses with full stops
source.statement: Don't end web or email addresses with full stops

compliant_examples: The People team manages the add a new employee form.

source.body_excerpt: Use full stops at the end of sentences with link text, but don’t include the full stop in the link itself.
heading_path: Ensure link text doesn’t include a full stop
source.statement: Ensure link text doesn't include a full stop

violating_examples: The People team manages the add a new employee form.
Don’t use full stops in:
Full stops do not go after:
symbols or
Use correct punctuation in government social media. You don’t need a full stop if your post ends in:
a web address (URL)
a tag or handle
a hashtag
an emoji
a sentence fragment.

source.body_excerpt:
In government text messages, use correct punctuation and grammar to avoid ambiguity. Correct writing shows people that the text is authoritative and trustworthy.

Include a full stop at the end of a text message if it finishes with a sentence. Don’t include a full stop if the message ends with a fragment or sign off.
heading_path: Punctuate text messages (SMS) correctly
source.statement: Punctuate text messages (SMS) correctly

source.body_excerpt: Hyphens clarify meaning by connecting words and parts of words into a single unit of meaning. Use hyphens to avoid ambiguity.
heading_path: Follow hyphenation rules in the dictionary your organisation uses
source.statement: Follow hyphenation rules in the dictionary your organisation uses

source.body_excerpt:
Hyphens are useful in some sets of words formed with prefixes such as:

- ‘anti-’
- ‘auto-’
- ‘counter-’
- ‘extra-’
- ‘intra-’
- ‘re-’
- ‘sub-’.

They’re especially useful for:

- doubled-up vowels
- clarifying new words that could be confused with existing ones.

A hyphen is used in some words with prefixes to distinguish them from words that would otherwise look the same.
heading_path: Write certain prefixes with a hyphen
source.statement: Write certain prefixes with a hyphen

source.body_excerpt:
Suffixes are normally attached directly to the base word without any hyphen. The commonest suffixes include:

- -able
- -ate
- -ation
- -fold
- -ful
- -ise
- -ish
- -ly
- -ment
- -ness
- -y.
heading_path: Write most suffixes without hyphens
source.statement: Write most suffixes without hyphens

source.body_excerpt:
A compound word consists of 2 or more words that carry a new meaning when used together.

Hyphens link elements of compound words as a phrase, but usually only when they are used before a noun as [adjectives](/node/126). Don’t use hyphens when the phrase is after the noun in the [sentence structure](/node/204).
heading_path: Hyphenate some but not all compound words
source.statement: Hyphenate some but not all compound words

source.body_excerpt: Hanging (or floating) hyphens connect 2 words to a base word or a number that they share.
heading_path: Repeat words instead of using a hanging hyphen
source.statement: Repeat words instead of using a hanging hyphen

source.body_excerpt: Don’t use a hyphen in most compounds consisting of an [adverb](/node/127) ending in ‘-ly’ and a participle (a part of a [verb](/node/128) ending in ‘-ing’ or ‘-ed’).
heading_path: Don’t hyphenate ‘-ing’ and ‘-ed’ verbs or most ‘-ly’ adverbs
source.statement: Don't hyphenate '-ing' and '-ed' verbs or most '-ly' adverbs

violating_examples: a fully-loaded truck
his rapidly-declining health
a partly-read book

source.body_excerpt:
Minimal punctuation doesn’t mean removing all punctuation marks from a sentence. It means removing unnecessary punctuation.

Only use punctuation that makes the sentence grammatically correct and the meaning clear.

Too much punctuation makes text crowded and difficult to read. If a sentence has a lot of punctuation marks, it might be a sign that the sentence is too long or complex. Try to rewrite into [shorter, clearer sentences](/node/204).

To use minimal punctuation:

- Don’t add full stops to the ends of headings, page headers, footers or captions.
- Don’t use a semicolon at the end of each item in a bullet list.
- Unless each item is a full sentence or the last item in a list, don’t use a full stop for
[items in bullet lists](/node/56). - Don’t use full stops between letters in an
[acronym or initialism](/node/190). - Don’t use a full stop at the end of most
[abbreviations](/node/184).

Minimal punctuation helps users understand your content.
heading_path: Use minimal punctuation to make meaning clear
source.statement: Use minimal punctuation to make meaning clear

source.body_excerpt:
Use punctuation marks to:

- end sentences (full stops, exclamation marks and question marks)
- break up sentences and show the relationship between words and phrases (commas, colons, semicolons, dashes, forward slashes and ellipses)
- show possession and contractions (apostrophes)
- connect related words (hyphens and dashes).
heading_path: Watch out for misplaced punctuation: it can change meaning
source.statement: Watch out for misplaced punctuation: it can change meaning

source.body_excerpt:
Check the relevant topic in this manual for advice on [how to treat each punctuation mark](/node/119).

There are different rules for putting spaces around punctuation marks. For example, some punctuation marks have no spaces around them. Some have a space on either side.

Include a single space after a punctuation mark at the end of a sentence. Never use double spaces. Check each document for double and multiple spaces and delete them.
heading_path: Use the correct spacing around punctuation marks
source.statement: Use the correct spacing around punctuation marks

source.body_excerpt:
Capitalise the first word in a sentence. Use lower case for all other words, unless those words include proper nouns. This is called ‘sentence case’.

Use sentence case for:

Do not use all capitals for headings, unless the visual design for the content meets WCAG in all respects.

Use sentence case with italics for titles of [works mentioned in the content](/node/181). This applies even when the reference is included in a heading within the content.
heading_path: Capitalise the first word in a sentence and in headings
source.statement: Capitalise the first word in a sentence and in headings

compliant_examples: Chief Defence Scientist Tanya Monro presented the award ...

source.body_excerpt:
Follow conventions for using capitals for [titles, honours and forms of address](/node/149). Use capitals when an official title precedes the name of the office holder. This includes titles for executives specified in legislation.

Unless advised in this manual, avoid using capitals in body text for a particular position or role within an organisation. This practice goes against readability and does not support clarity.

You do not need to use capitals when the title is an organisational name given to an office holder. Deference for positions within an organisation might follow house style. Do not use house style outside of the organisational context. Detail any special use of capitals in a [style sheet](/node/169#a_style_sheet_is_a_useful_tool).

Preferences for capitals when the terms ‘traditional owner’, ‘elder’ and ‘custodian’ are used as titles should come directly from the relevant [First Nations community](/node/179#style_for_first_australian_languages_needs_to_recognise_continuing_cultures).
heading_path: Follow the guidance on capitals for titles and government terms
source.statement: Follow the guidance on capitals for titles and government terms

violating_examples: The Senior Policy Adviser offered their view ...
Follow the rules of capitalisation for government terms, for example:
government programs and agreements
mentions of parliament
references to states and territories.
Legal material has its own conventions for capitalisation. Content that has a legislative focus might use complementary sources to the guidance on citing legal material in this manual.

Legal documents often use initial capitals to show terms with a defined meaning (such as ‘Department’, ‘Schedule’, ‘Vendor’ and ‘Recipient’). In these cases, use the form of the name as it is written in the legislation.

source.body_excerpt: Question marks can express doubt and uncertainty about dates or other specific details.
heading_path: She asked, ‘Is the report due on Tuesday?’
Inserted question marks can show uncertainty
source.statement: Inserted question marks can show uncertainty

source.body_excerpt:
Quotations that are longer than about 30 words are:

- usually indented from the text margin
- sometimes set in a smaller font size or a different font.

When they are set like this, they are called* *‘block quotations’.

Don’t use quotation marks to identify the quoted material – the formatting does that instead. Block quotations should also be coded with the HTML <blockquote> element.
heading_path: Format long quotes as block quotations with no quotation marks
source.statement: Format long quotes as block quotations with no quotation marks

source.body_excerpt: Quotation marks are unnecessary in transcripts and plays if the name of the speaker comes before the direct speech.
heading_path: Write speech in transcripts and plays with no quotation marks
source.statement: Write speech in transcripts and plays with no quotation marks

source.body_excerpt:
When referring to these titles, use quotation marks in [references and citations](/node/181):

- a chapter in a book or report
- an article in a periodical
- an essay
- a lecture
- a poem
- a song.
heading_path: Refer to certain kinds of titles using quotation marks
source.statement: Refer to certain kinds of titles using quotation marks

compliant_examples: Did you hear him say, ‘That’s unlikely’?

source.body_excerpt:
Punctuation in and after quotation marks depends on the punctuation of the quoted text and how it is used in the content.

If the punctuation mark is part of the quoted text, place the punctuation mark before the closing quotation mark.
heading_path: Keep quoted punctuation marks in the quote
source.statement: Keep quoted punctuation marks in the quote

violating_examples: The Speaker called ‘Order!’.
Did you hear him say, ‘That’s unlikely.’?

The surrounding text determines the font (roman, italic, or bold) of the quotation marks. If the content inside the quotation marks is in italics, but the sentence is in roman, use roman for the quotation marks.

compliant_examples: Find out if it’s optional or compulsory before you start. Ask someone to help you if you don’t know the difference.
Staff can leave at any time; they don’t need a work schedule.

source.body_excerpt:
Short, simple sentences are easier to read. Overusing semicolons makes writing more difficult to understand.

Semicolons can create a break that is stronger than a comma but weaker than a full stop. They can link 2 sentences that share or develop an idea. The information must be closely related.
heading_path: Avoid using a semicolon to link sentences
source.statement: Avoid using a semicolon to link sentences

violating_examples: Find out if it’s optional or compulsory before you start; ask someone to help you if you don’t know the difference.

Too much punctuation makes text crowded and difficult to read. If a sentence has a lot of punctuation marks, it might be a sign that the sentence is too long or complex. Try to rewrite into shorter, clearer sentences.
If you have to use a semicolon, on both sides of the semicolon write full sentences. Other than in some sentence lists, it’s incorrect to have a sentence fragment on one side of the semicolon.
Staff can leave at any time; no work schedule.

source.body_excerpt: You don’t need a semicolon at the end of each list item for bullet and numbered [lists](/node/56). It clutters the list and makes it hard to read.
heading_path: Don’t end bullet and numbered list items with semicolons
source.statement: Don't end bullet and numbered list items with semicolons

violating_examples: The successful applicant will demonstrate:
integrity, persistence and good judgement;
experience in projects of this type; and
a sound understanding of interdepartmental relationships.

source.body_excerpt: Use a semicolon between each reference when you have more than one in-text [reference in brackets](/node/181).
heading_path: Separate in-text references with semicolons
source.statement: Separate in-text references with semicolons

source.body_excerpt:
Complex lists in sentences can be hard to read. If you can’t use a bullet or numbered list, separate list items with:

- commas if the list is simple, such as a list of single words
- semicolons if the list is complex, such as a list of items that already contain commas or conjunctions.

In complex lists, you need semicolons to show what goes with what.

It is almost always better to break a complex list into a bullet or numbered list to make it easier to read.
heading_path: Use a bullet or numbered list instead of semicolons in a complex sentence
source.statement: Use a bullet or numbered list instead of semicolons in a complex sentence

source.body_excerpt: Abbreviations contain the first single letter or first few letters of a word. They don’t include the last letter of a word.
heading_path: Limit the use of abbreviations
source.statement: Limit the use of abbreviations

violating_examples: Thank you for your email about errors in the third para of the webpage *How to apply for a special use permit*.
Abbreviations are useful in very limited circumstances:
in a table or chart, where space is unavailable for the full form of the word – provide a note under the table or chart giving the full form
when using ‘cont’ to show continuing text in another part of content (for example, on another page of a print newsletter) – the full form of the word is more helpful where space allows.
Semi-formal and informal content uses abbreviations more often. Use abbreviations only if users will understand what they mean. If there’s any doubt, define the abbreviation on first use.
Avoid using abbreviations in any public-facing content.

source.body_excerpt:
Don’t place a full stop after an abbreviation.

There are exceptions:

- when the abbreviation ends a sentence and isn’t followed by another punctuation mark
- for abbreviations of scientific names for
[plants and animals](/node/96) - for the abbreviation ‘n.d.’(meaning ‘no date’) for the year of publication in references.
heading_path: Don’t put a full stop after most abbreviations
source.statement: Don't put a full stop after most abbreviations

source.body_excerpt: Use the same capitalisation as for the unabbreviated word.
heading_path: Capitalise the same way as the spelt-out version
source.statement: Capitalise the same way as the spelt-out version

source.body_excerpt: Write out the abbreviated term in full.
heading_path: Don’t abbreviate the first word in a sentence
source.statement: Don't abbreviate the first word in a sentence

source.body_excerpt: Add an ‘s’. One exception is ‘pp’* *(pages), which is used when referring to multiple pages.
heading_path: Add ‘s’ to create plural abbreviations
source.statement: Add 's' to create plural abbreviations

source.body_excerpt: Acronyms comprise the initial letters (and sometimes syllables) of the words in a term and are pronounced as a word.
heading_path: Choose acronyms and initialisms people will recognise
source.statement: Choose acronyms and initialisms people will recognise

source.body_excerpt:
People unfamiliar with certain terms might not understand their shortened forms. Acronyms and initialisms might also be misread by screen readers.

To make sure all shortened forms are accessible:

- Define them the first time you use them in content (unless you’re certain all users will understand them without a definition – consult a dictionary first).
- Include them with their spelt-out forms in the glossary. This is particularly important if the content contains many specialist shortened forms.
heading_path: Explain acronyms and initialisms to all users
source.statement: Explain acronyms and initialisms to all users

source.body_excerpt: If there’s a chance users won’t know the meaning of an acronym or initialism, define it at first mention. Write the term in full first and follow with the acronym or initialism in parentheses. Use the shortened form rather than the full term for later mentions.
heading_path: Explain acronyms and initialisms to all users
Spell out most acronyms on first use
source.statement: Spell out most acronyms on first use

source.body_excerpt:
If you use the shortened form only a few times in long-form content, consider writing out the full term more than once.

People could come across the shortened form without reading the text where it is first defined. For example, a user might click straight to a section that only includes the shortened form.
heading_path: Explain acronyms and initialisms to all users
Repeat the full term if the user needs it
source.statement: Repeat the full term if the user needs it

source.body_excerpt: The names of government departments are often shortened, but not always in the same way.
heading_path: Check the correct shortened form for government organisations
source.statement: Check the correct shortened form for government organisations

source.body_excerpt:
For content with many specialised acronyms and initialisms, provide a glossary – a list of terms and their meaning that users can refer to.

Include the glossary at the end of the content or on a separate webpage. Use a hyperlink in the text to help people access the glossary.

You don’t need to include a glossary if:

- there are only a few unfamiliar shortened forms
- each one is only in a very limited section of text
- each one is spelt out when first mentioned.
heading_path: Include a list if content relies on many acronyms and initialisms
source.statement: Include a list if content relies on many acronyms and initialisms

source.body_excerpt:
Don’t place a full stop after the acronym or initialism.

The exception is if the shortened form ends a sentence and isn’t followed by another punctuation mark.
heading_path: Don’t end acronyms and initialisms with a full stop
source.statement: Don't end acronyms and initialisms with a full stop

source.body_excerpt:
Acronyms are usually all capitals, but use lower case for some familiar acronyms (taser, captcha, laser). Use an initial capital for familiar acronyms that are proper nouns (Qantas, Anzac).

Initialisms are often all upper case (VOIP, FOI) but there are exceptions (bpm). Consult a dictionary if you’re unsure of the capitalisation.

If the acronym or initialism represents common nouns, don’t begin each word of the full form with a capital letter.
heading_path: Use capitals for most acronyms and initialisms
source.statement: Use capitals for most acronyms and initialisms

source.body_excerpt: Avoid using the plural or possessive of an acronym or initialism when you define it. This makes it easy for users to recognise the shortened form in later content.
heading_path: Avoid plural and possessive forms on the first use
source.statement: Avoid plural and possessive forms on the first use

source.body_excerpt: Single-word contractions use the first and last letters of a word and sometimes other letters in between.
heading_path: Shorten single words and grammatical phrases with care
source.statement: Shorten single words and grammatical phrases with care

source.body_excerpt: Don’t place a full stop after contractions. The exception is when the contraction ends a sentence and isn’t followed by another punctuation mark.
heading_path: Don’t end contractions with full stops
source.statement: Don't end contractions with full stops

violating_examples: sha’n’t

source.body_excerpt: Use the capitalisation that you would use for the uncontracted word. Capitalisation of the uncontracted word depends on the context.
heading_path: Capitalise contractions in the same way as the full word
source.statement: Capitalise contractions in the same way as the full word

source.body_excerpt: Write out the contracted term in full unless it’s a grammatical contraction.
heading_path: Use the full word at start of the sentence (except for grammatical contractions)
source.statement: Use the full word at start of the sentence (except for grammatical contractions)

source.body_excerpt:
Use Latin forms only in limited situations – for example:

- where there’s limited space, such as in tables
- in technical and specialist publications that use them.

| Shortened form | Complete Latin word | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| c. | circa |
about, approximately |
| cf. | conferatur |
compare |
| e.g. | exempli gratia |
for example |
| et al. | et alii |
and others |
| etc. | et cetera |
and so forth, and so on |
| i.e. | id est |
that is |
| MS | manuscriptum |
manuscript |
| NB | nota bene |
take careful note |
| PPS | post postscriptum |
second postscript |
| PS | postscriptum |
postscript |
| v., vs | versus |
against |
| viz. | videlicet |
namely |

Unlike other shortened forms, some Latin shortened forms have full stops.

The terms ‘i.e.’ and ‘e.g.’ need full stops after each letter. This helps screen readers announce them.

Don’t follow ‘e.g.’ or ‘i.e.’ with a comma, regardless of whether you would use a comma in the sentence.
heading_path: Avoid using Latin shortened forms in most content
source.statement: Avoid using Latin shortened forms in most content

compliant_examples: This funding is intended for upgrading roads in Gold Coast and Hinterland urban centres (for example, Surfers Paradise and Southport).
This funding is for upgrading roads in the Gold Coast and Hinterland urban centres (Surfers Paradise, Southport, Upper Coomera and Robina).

source.body_excerpt: Rather than using ‘e.g.’ or ‘i.e.’ write the English words out in full. Write ‘for example’ and ‘that is’ instead, particularly in more formal publications.
heading_path: Use the English words where possible
source.statement: Use the English words where possible

violating_examples: They found some aspects of grammar confusing, e.g. the different types of pronouns.
The department has a major problem with its website, i.e. users find pages very slow to load.
Don’t use the shortened form for *et cetera*. Use of ‘etc.’ is redundant in a list introduced by ‘for example’, ‘such as’ or ‘including’. These expressions show that the list is incomplete.
If you think you need to include ‘etc.’ because there’s more to say, include these ideas in your sentence instead.
This funding is for upgrading roads in Gold Coast and Hinterland urban centres (for example, Surfers Paradise, Southport etc.).

source.body_excerpt:
Government organisations should choose one dictionary of Australian English.

This manual recommends either:

- the
*Australian concise Oxford dictionary*(ACOD) - the
*Macquarie dictionary*.

Use your organisation’s preferred dictionary as a spelling reference when you write. Spelling and word usage can change over time. Make sure you use an up-to-date edition that reflects current language usages.

Dictionaries include any variable spellings for words. Always use the first entry in the list. This helps to ensure words are spelt consistently in government content.

Only use an alternative spelling listed for a word if you have evidence it will meet a [user need](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/user-needs/understanding-needs/user-research-and-content). Record decisions you make about alternative spellings in a [style sheet](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/style-rules-and-conventions/general-conventions-editing-and-proofreading/editing-and-proofreading#a_style_sheet_is_a_useful_tool).

The entry for a spelling can expand on changes to the basic form of a word. These changes show things like the plural, past tense, or the root from which a word is formed. These changes are called ‘infle
heading_path: Choose one dictionary for consistency
source.statement: Choose one dictionary for consistency

source.body_excerpt:
The Style Manual has specific guidance about writing certain terms and phrases correctly.

Follow our guidance for:

There is also guidance related to spelling at [punctuation and capitalisation](/node/116).
heading_path: Follow guidance in this manual
source.statement: Follow guidance in this manual

source.body_excerpt:
The spelling of some words is variable. Sometimes it’s difficult to know which spelling or word to use because:

- Australian, American and British English have different ways of spelling a word
- a word might sound similar to another, so people can mishear it and write the wrong word.

Follow one dictionary for consistency and use it to check variable [spellings](/node/30).
heading_path: Check for words that are easily confused or misspelt
source.statement: Check for words that are easily confused or misspelt

source.body_excerpt:
Correct word use makes content readable and clear to users. Getting words wrong risks losing users’ engagement with, and trust of, your content.

This alphabetical list contains some of the words that people get wrong in government writing. Check your dictionary for the full set of meanings of each word.
heading_path: Choose the right word and spell it correctly
source.statement: Choose the right word and spell it correctly

source.body_excerpt:
The academic and professional titles held by individuals usually have initial capitals. This includes honorary titles.

Use lower case if you use a title [generically](#generic).
heading_path: Use initial capitals for the titles of individual academics and professionals
source.statement: Use initial capitals for the titles of individual academics and professionals

source.body_excerpt:
Academics and professionals are often addressed by their ‘full title’. A full title includes the title or honorific (with initial capitals), name, post-nominals, position and organisation.

Use a full title:

- to introduce an individual as speaker
- in address and signature blocks in correspondence
- in official records of proceedings
- in lists in organisational publications such as annual reports
- if it is important to know where an individual works.

A full title is often about using titles in a display or presentation context (display text).
heading_path: Use full titles in certain contexts
source.statement: Use full titles in certain contexts

source.body_excerpt:
Generic use of academic and professional titles includes:

- titles that describe a named individual
- plural titles
- common nouns.

As shown in the previous section, most titles that appear after a name are generic.

Some titles appearing immediately before a name are also generic because they describe the individual. These titles are usually preceded by ‘the’ or a modifier. Adjectives are modifiers because they restrict the meaning of a noun.
heading_path: Use lower case for titles used in a generic way
source.statement: Use lower case for titles used in a generic way

compliant_examples: This year’s graduate cohort asked Deputy Vice-Chancellor Jonquil Johansson to moderate their debate.

source.body_excerpt:
When you write about an individual, it’s respectful to use their title.

The first time you mention someone in body text, use their academic or professional title before their first name and last name, followed by post-nominals.

If you mention the individual again, only use the title and last name. Some academic titles have an accepted abbreviated title you can use after the first mention.
heading_path: Use title, name and post-nominals at first mention
source.statement: Use title, name and post-nominals at first mention

violating_examples: DVC Jonquil Johansson to moderate their debate.

source.body_excerpt:
Post-nominals are letters after a name that stand for academic, civil and military [awards and honours](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/style-rules-and-conventions/titles-honours-forms-address/awards-and-honours).

Make sure you write post-nominals [in the right order](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/style-rules-and-conventions/titles-honours-forms-address/awards-and-honours#use_postnominals_in_the_correct_order).

Don’t use commas before or between post-nominals.
heading_path: Write post-nominals after the name in academic and professional titles
source.statement: Write post-nominals after the name in academic and professional titles

source.body_excerpt:
The first time you write a name in body text, use the academic and professional title along with the first and last name. Include the post-nominal for a civil or military honour in the title.

If you mention the name again, use the title and last name, but don’t include the post-nominal.
heading_path: Write post-nominals after the name in academic and professional titles
Use post-nominals at first mention only
source.statement: Use post-nominals at first mention only

source.body_excerpt: Retain any post-nominals for civil and military honours when using the shortened forms of titles.
heading_path: Write post-nominals after the name in academic and professional titles
Include post-nominals in the shortened forms of titles
source.statement: Include post-nominals in the shortened forms of titles

source.body_excerpt:
Post-nominals can also stand for tertiary and professional qualifications.

Use these post-nominals:

- for correspondence within the academic community
- to show relevant expertise.

Don’t include both ‘Dr’ (doctorate) and ‘PhD’ (Doctor of Philosophy) for the one name. It is conventional to use either the title or the post-nominal. This also applies to PhD equivalents such as ‘LLD’ (Doctor of Laws).

Don’t include post-nominals for master and bachelor degrees in correspondence.
heading_path: Write post-nominals after the name in academic and professional titles
Use post-nominals for academic and professional qualifications in 2 contexts
source.statement: Use post-nominals for academic and professional qualifications in 2 contexts

source.body_excerpt:
Use ‘RAN’ (Royal Australian Navy) for all commissioned officers of the Navy. Place ‘RAN’ after the family name and any post-nominals.

Don’t use an acronym to show service for officers in the Army or Air Force.

In Defence, ‘RAN’ is used to distinguish naval officers from officers in the other services and from naval officers in other countries.

Gazettal notices of Australian awards and honours follow this style. For consistency, the Style Manual recommends that Australian Government organisations also follow this practice.
heading_path: Use ‘RAN’ to indicate Navy service for commissioned officers
source.statement: Use 'RAN' to indicate Navy service for commissioned officers

source.body_excerpt: When someone has a military rank and another title such as ‘Sir’, ‘Dame’ or ‘the Honourable’, place the military rank first.
heading_path: Write the rank before the title of ADF members who are knighted
source.statement: Write the rank before the title of ADF members who are knighted

source.body_excerpt:
Post-nominals are the shortened forms for academic awards and civil and military honours.

There is an [order in which to write the post-nominals](https://www.pmc.gov.au/resource-centre/government/post-nominals).

In summary, the rule is to write the highest honour first. The order is:

- post-nominals for honours and awards
- King’s Counsel (KC) or Senior Counsel (SC) or Justice of the Peace (JP)
- university degrees and diplomas
- membership of professional associations
- membership of parliament.

Don’t use:

- full stops or spaces within post-nominals
- commas before or between post-nominals.
heading_path: Use post-nominals in the correct order
source.statement: Use post-nominals in the correct order

source.body_excerpt:
Vice-regal and ecclesiastical titles and Australian Defence Force ranks usually precede all other titles.

Follow these with any other titles (such as ‘Dame’, ‘Sir’ and ‘Dr’) immediately before a person’s name.
heading_path: Write titles before a person’s name in the correct order
source.statement: Write titles before a person's name in the correct order

source.body_excerpt:
The title for diplomats depends on what they represent:

- High commissioners represent Commonwealth countries.
- Ambassadors represent non-Commonwealth countries.
- Nuncios represent the Holy See, the governing body of the Roman Catholic Church.
heading_path: Use the correct term when referring to diplomats
source.statement: Use the correct term when referring to diplomats

source.body_excerpt: Use initial capitals when writing to ambassadors, high commissioners and nuncios.
heading_path: Use the correct term when referring to diplomats
Use initial capitals for the titles of high commissioners, ambassadors and nuncios
source.statement: Use initial capitals for the titles of high commissioners, ambassadors and nuncios

source.body_excerpt:
Refer to judges of the following courts as ‘Justice’ and use the title ‘The Honourable’:

- High Court
- Federal Court
- Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 1)
- supreme courts in the states and territories.

Use the titles ‘Your Honour’, ‘His Honour’ or ‘Her Honour’ for judges of:

- Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2)
- district courts
- county courts.
heading_path: Use the correct form to refer to judges and magistrates
source.statement: Use the correct form to refer to judges and magistrates

source.body_excerpt:
Capitalise the titles of the current holders of the positions of:

- Prime Minister
- Treasurer.

Do this even when the titles are abbreviated.

If referencing prime ministers or treasurers generically, use lower case.
heading_path: Capitalise the titles of the current prime minister and treasurer
source.statement: Capitalise the titles of the current prime minister and treasurer

source.body_excerpt:
The Parliament of Australia website has instructions for [how to address senators and members](https://www.aph.gov.au/Senators_and_Members/Contacting_Senators_and_Members/How_to_address_Senators_and_Members).

Write these titles as follows:

- the Prime Minister
- the President of the Senate
- the Speaker of the House of Representatives
- ministers (Senate)
- ministers (House of Representatives)
- assistant ministers (Senate)
- assistant ministers (House of Representatives)
- senators
- members (House of Representatives).

People elected to the upper house take the title ‘Senator’ before their given name.
heading_path: Capitalise titles for current senators and members of the Australian Parliament
source.statement: Capitalise titles for current senators and members of the Australian Parliament

source.body_excerpt: In formal emails and letters, address members of state and territory parliaments with the relevant post-nominal after their name.
heading_path: Use the appropriate form for members of state and territory parliaments
source.statement: Use the appropriate form for members of state and territory parliaments

source.body_excerpt:
The parliaments of all states except Qld are ‘bicameral’. This means parliament has 2 chambers or houses:

- the Legislative Council – also called the ‘upper house’
- the Legislative Assembly (NSW, Vic and WA) or House of Assembly (SA and Tas) – also called the ‘lower house’.

The parliaments of Qld, the ACT and the NT are ‘unicameral’. This means parliament has one chamber or house – the Legislative Assembly.
heading_path: Use the appropriate form for members of state and territory parliaments
Number of chambers in state and territory parliament
source.statement: Number of chambers in state and territory parliament

source.body_excerpt:
Members of state and territory parliaments use the post-nominal:

- MLC (Member of the Legislative Council)
- MLA (Member of the Legislative Assembly)
- MP (Member of the Legislative Assembly or Member of the House of Assembly).

All bicameral parliaments use the post-nominal 'MLC' for members of their upper houses.

The choice of 'MLA' or 'MP' for members of state and territory parliaments is less clear-cut.

Follow these rules to use the correct post-nominal.

Use MLC for members of the Legislative Council of:

- NSW
- SA
- Tas
- Vic
- WA.

Use MLA for members of the Legislative Assembly of:

- ACT
- NT
- WA.

Use MP for members of the Legislative Assembly of:

- NSW
- Qld
- Vic.

Use MP for members of the House of Assembly of:

- SA
- Tas.
heading_path: Use the appropriate form for members of state and territory parliaments
Use the correct post-nominal
source.statement: Use the correct post-nominal

source.body_excerpt:
Regnal numbers are upper case roman numerals that are used for the titles of monarchs and popes.

Don’t use digits or ordinal numbers, even though you might pronounce them like that.
heading_path: Use regnal numbers (I, II, V) for titles of monarchs and religious leaders
source.statement: Use regnal numbers (I, II, V) for titles of monarchs and religious leaders

violating_examples: Margrethe the second
Rama 9
Gewargis the 3rd

source.body_excerpt:
Put a non-breaking space between the name and the regnal number. A non-breaking space means that line breaks won’t split up both elements of the name. The name and number will stay together on one line.

You can insert a non-breaking space using the Unicode character U+00A0.

In HTML, use the entity to insert a non-breaking space. You can also use the keyboard shortcut Ctrl+Shift+Spacebar in Word.
heading_path: Use regnal numbers (I, II, V) for titles of monarchs and religious leaders
Use a non-breaking space for names with regnal numbers
source.statement: Use a non-breaking space for names with regnal numbers

source.body_excerpt:
The position of governor-general in Australia is known as vice-royalty. The Governor-General represents the King in Australia.

Address the Governor-General of Australia in the following style and order:

- ‘His/Her Excellency the Honourable’
- prefixed titles
- given name and family name
- post-nominals
- ‘Governor-General of the Commonwealth of Australia’.

You might need to vary the order of the items in the title to suit the titles of the incumbent. For example, place:

- military rank before ‘the Honourable’
- ‘Sir’ or ‘Dame’ after ‘the Honourable’.
heading_path: Capitalise ‘Governor-General’ when it’s part of the formal title
source.statement: Capitalise 'Governor-General' when it's part of the formal title

source.body_excerpt:
Use adjectives sparingly and only when they are essential for meaning. Remove any adjective that doesn’t play a critical function in a [sentence](/node/204).

Because adjectives are modifiers, they can affect clarity. A lack of clarity can cause users to lose trust in government content.
heading_path: Adjectives can affect clarity
source.statement: Adjectives can affect clarity

compliant_examples: A badly worded sentence can be difficult to read, even if it is grammatically correct.

source.body_excerpt: Adjectives can be joined with [hyphens to make compound adjectives](/node/105#use_hyphens_for_some_compound_words). A compound adjective usually has a hyphen if the adjective is before the noun it is describing.
heading_path: Compound adjectives can have hyphens
source.statement: Compound adjectives can have hyphens

violating_examples: A badly-worded sentence can be difficult to read, even if it is grammatically-correct.
There are few exceptions to this rule, so check a dictionary if you are unsure.

source.body_excerpt:
Use adverbs sparingly. Remove any adverb that doesn’t play a critical function in a [sentence](/node/204).

Because adverbs are modifiers, they can affect clarity. A lack of clarity can cause users to lose trust in government content.
heading_path: Adverbs can affect clarity
source.statement: Adverbs can affect clarity

source.body_excerpt:
Some pronouns introduce nouns, so they work as determiners. Examples of these pronouns are ‘any’, ‘some’, ‘this’, ‘that’, ‘these’, ‘those’, ‘my’, ‘your’, ‘his’, ‘her’.

Pronouns, working as determiners, can show which noun you are referring to.
heading_path: Pronouns can function as determiners
source.statement: Pronouns can function as determiners

source.body_excerpt: Numbers work as determiners because they give information about how many nouns they are introducing.
heading_path: Numbers can function as determiners
source.statement: Numbers can function as determiners

source.body_excerpt: Concrete nouns name things you can identify through one or more of the 5 senses.
heading_path: Common nouns can be concrete or abstract
source.statement: Common nouns can be concrete or abstract

source.body_excerpt: Nouns can be singular or plural. Most English words add an ‘-s’ or ‘-es’ to form the plural, but there are many exceptions. Check a dictionary if you’re not sure.
heading_path: Nouns can be singular or plural
source.statement: Nouns can be singular or plural

violating_examples: Adjust the desk’s and chair’s.

source.body_excerpt:
You can sort nouns by whether they can be separated into individual units and counted:

- You can count countable nouns.
- You cannot count uncountable nouns.
heading_path: Nouns can be countable or uncountable
source.statement: Nouns can be countable or uncountable

violating_examples: Report is being printed.
An uncountable noun has no plural and only a singular verb. Uncountable nouns don’t need to have a determiner. Whether it has one depends on the meaning of the sentence.

compliant_examples: The analyst works in the office on Mondays.

source.body_excerpt: The form of the verb changes to show whether the subject is singular or plural (the number). This is called ‘subject–verb agreement’.
heading_path: Verbs must ‘agree’ with the subject
source.statement: Verbs must 'agree' with the subject

violating_examples: Jan work in the office on Mondays.
To decide which form of the verb you need, find its subject and ask ‘who’ or ‘what’ is doing the verb. Using the first example:
Question: Who works in the office on Mondays?
Answer: The analyst.
This answer might seem obvious, but subject–verb agreement is not always intuitive. For example, a common mistake is to use the plural form of a verb with a collective noun.

Sentences contain at least a subject and a verb. Keep the relationship between the grammatical subject and the verb clear to users. This relationship is the basis for writing plain language sentences.

source.body_excerpt: Rule: Author A or Agency Name (Year) *Title of report: subtitle of report*, Name of Agency, Name of Government, accessed Day Month Year.
heading_path: Reports
Report by an Australian government agency
source.statement: Report by an Australian government agency

source.body_excerpt: Rule: Author A or Agency Name (Year) ‘Title of report: subtitle of report’, *Name of Series*, catalogue number, Name of Agency, Name of Government, accessed Day Month Year.
heading_path: Reports
Report that is part of a series
source.statement: Report that is part of a series

source.body_excerpt: Rule: Author A or Agency Name (Year) *Title of report: subtitle of report*, report to Agency Name, Organisation Name or Abbreviation.
heading_path: Reports
Report to an Australian government agency
source.statement: Report to an Australian government agency

source.body_excerpt:
Sometimes a report is better known by a short title or unofficial title. If you’re citing a source like this, use the short title in text.

In the reference list, use the short title followed by a spaced en dash and the full source information. List the source where the first word of the short title would be alphabetically.
heading_path: Reports
Report known by a short title
source.statement: Report known by a short title

source.body_excerpt:
Only include the place of publication if it’s relevant to the user.

The place of publication may be relevant if:

- you cite works with editions published in multiple locations
- the location where the book was published affects the credibility of your work.

Editions of books published in different locations may have different spelling conventions. For example, the same publisher may publish an edition in London (using UK spelling) and an edition in New York (using US spelling).

Sometimes knowing the place of publication of the sources adds credibility to the work. For example, an Australian publication may be more credible if it cites books published in Australia. Including the publishing location clearly shows users where the book is from.

If the place of publication doesn’t add useful information for the user, you can omit it from your citation.
heading_path: Books
Place of publication of a book
source.statement: Place of publication of a book

source.body_excerpt:
Electronic media include film, television, radio and podcasts. When you write about electronic media you could also be referring to a script or a review.

Many of the general naming rules apply:

- Use sentence case – retain initial capitals for the first word, proper nouns and proper adjectives.
- Use italics for published works and roman type for unpublished works.
- Use roman type and quotation marks for parts of works, such as episodes.
- Use roman type and the spelling and capitalisation that the company uses for the names of channels, streaming services and networks.
- Use full names of organisations the first time you mention them.

Italicise the titles of films, television and radio programs, and podcasts.

Place the names of episodes in quotation marks and roman type.

Examples of in-text citations and reference lists on this page follow the author–date system, as this is the most common way of citing film, television and radio programs in government content.
heading_path: Cite electronic media correctly
source.statement: Cite electronic media correctly

source.body_excerpt:
Write the title as it appears in film information. Include punctuation marks and any intentional misspelling. Italicise the title and use sentence case.

If the film is part of a series, include the number of the series in the same format as in the original title of the film. For example, if the original title has the number written as a word, use the word.

In-text citations of films often include the year of production. Place this after the title in roman type and enclosed in parentheses.

If you mention the date in the text, you don’t have to include it in parentheses.
heading_path: Use italics and sentence case for film titles
source.statement: Use italics and sentence case for film titles

source.body_excerpt:
In a reference list, use the director and the year of release. Include the place of production if known. If there is no credited director, use the name of the producer.

Rule: Director D (director) or Producer P (producer) (Year) *Title of film: subtitle of film* [motion picture], Name of Studio or Publisher, Place of Production.
heading_path: Use italics and sentence case for film titles
Reference list entries for films
source.statement: Reference list entries for films

source.body_excerpt:
Use sentence case, roman type and quotation marks for episodes of a program.

Use roman type and no quotation marks for the names of:

- production companies
- networks
- channels
- streaming services.

Include the year of production of television programs in roman type and brackets.
heading_path: Italicise television programs
source.statement: Italicise television programs

violating_examples: Season II of *Offspring* introduced the character of Dr Patrick Reid.

source.body_excerpt:
In a reference list, include the name of the director or producer and the year of release. Include the place of production if known.

Rule: Director D (director) or Producer P (producer) (Year) ‘Title of episode: subtitle of episode’ [television program], *Name of series* (season number, episode number), Name of Station or Studio, Place of Production.
heading_path: Italicise television programs
Reference list entries for television programs
source.statement: Reference list entries for television programs

source.body_excerpt:
To cite radio programs:

- Use italics for the titles of programs.
- Write the year of production in parentheses. Use roman type after the title.
- Enclose the names of individual episodes in single quotation marks and use roman type.
- Use sentence case.
heading_path: Italicise radio programs and use roman type for episodes
source.statement: Italicise radio programs and use roman type for episodes

source.body_excerpt:
In a reference list, include the full date the episode went to air. Include the place of production if known.

Rule: Presenter P (presenter) (Day Month Year) ‘Title of episode: subtitle of episode’ [radio program], *Name of program*, Name of Station or Studio, Place of Production.
heading_path: Italicise radio programs and use roman type for episodes
Reference list entries for radio programs
source.statement: Reference list entries for radio programs

source.body_excerpt:
To cite podcasts:

- Use italics for the name of the program series.
- Use roman type and quotation marks for the names of individual podcast episodes.
- Use sentence case.
heading_path: Italicise podcast series and use roman type for episodes
source.statement: Italicise podcast series and use roman type for episodes

source.body_excerpt:
Hyperlink the episode’s title if you played it from a webpage. Don’t link to the podcast’s file name. Always link to the webpage that hosts the podcast episode. Include the date it was accessed at the end of the reference.

Rule: Host H (host) and Producer P (producer) (Day Month Year) ‘Title of podcast: subtitle of podcast’ [podcast], *Name of podcast*, Name of Podcast Network, accessed Day Month Year.
heading_path: Italicise podcast series and use roman type for episodes
Reference list entries for podcasts
source.statement: Reference list entries for podcasts

source.body_excerpt:
Published script titles follow the same rules as book titles:

- Use italics and sentence case for published script titles.
- Use roman type and quotation marks for unpublished script titles.
heading_path: Apply the same rules for script titles as for books
source.statement: Apply the same rules for script titles as for books

source.body_excerpt:
Reference the script as you would a book.

Rule: Author A (Year) *Title of script: subtitle of script*, Name of Publisher, Place of Publication.
heading_path: Apply the same rules for script titles as for books
Reference list entries for scripts
source.statement: Reference list entries for scripts

source.body_excerpt:
Write titles of published reviews in roman type enclosed in single quotation marks. Write the title of the reviewed material in italics and use sentence case.

You may be able to hyperlink to the online review, depending on copyright restrictions. If you access it online, include an accessed date.
heading_path: Use roman type and quotation marks for review titles
source.statement: Use roman type and quotation marks for review titles

source.body_excerpt:
If the name of the reviewed work appears in the title of the review, use italics for the work name but roman type for the rest of the title.

Rule: Reviewer R (Day Month Year) ‘Title of review: subtitle of review’ [review of *Title of work* by Creator], *Name of Blog, Newspaper or Magazine*, accessed Day Month Year.
heading_path: Use roman type and quotation marks for review titles
Reference list entries for reviews
source.statement: Reference list entries for reviews

source.body_excerpt:
Disciplines and sources define the term ‘classics’ in different ways. This guidance covers ancient Greek and Roman works (until the 5th century) and works from the medieval period (from the fall of the Roman empire until the middle of the 15th century).

In references and in-text citations, treat the titles of classics as you would other book titles.

- Use sentence case – capitalise only the first letter of the title and the first letter of any proper noun.
- Use italics for the titles of books, series and anthologies.
- Use quotation marks for the titles of chapters, poems or sections.

If you’re using a reference list, include any classics that you cite.

Examples of in-text citations and reference lists on this page follow the author–date system, as this is the most common way of citing the classics in government content. If your organisation uses the documentary–note system, change the citation and style of reference list accordingly.
heading_path: Cite classics as book titles
source.statement: Cite classics as book titles

compliant_examples: As Cicero expressed it, ‘Is there anything rasher and more unworthy of the dignity and strength of character of a wise man than the holding of a false opinion?’ (*On the nature of the gods*)

source.body_excerpt:
Often there will not be much information for classics. For example, you might not know the date of publication.

Include the information that you know in in-text citations.

If you don’t know the name of the author, don’t use ‘Anon’*, *‘unknown’ or ‘Anonymous’ in the in-text citation.
heading_path: Use correct in-text citations
source.statement: Use correct in-text citations

violating_examples: Beowulf*(Anon) is the story of a hero who defeats a dragon.- Like Grendel (Anonymous
Beowulf*), you seem to suffer with the joy of others.
If you don’t know the author or the date of a work, use the name of the translator (trans) and the date of publication of the edition you’re working with. Place the date at the end of the reference.

As Marcus Tullius Cicero expressed it, ‘Is there anything rasher and more unworthy of the dignity and strength of character of a wise man than the holding of a false opinion?’ (*On the nature of the gods*)

source.body_excerpt: Some classics have divisions. Divisions organise prose and poetry into, for example, books, chapters, sections, lines and verses.
heading_path: Include divisions in in-text citations when possible
source.statement: Include divisions in in-text citations when possible

source.body_excerpt:
Most of the time, you’ll be working with translations. The exception is when you’re quoting text in the original language.

**Accessibility requirements**

If any text should be pronounced in its original language (rather than English), screen readers need to be able to determine what that language is.

WCAG quick reference: [3.1.2 Language of parts – level AA](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/quickref/?showtechniques=312%2C131#language-of-parts)
heading_path: Cite titles in the most appropriate language
source.statement: Cite titles in the most appropriate language

source.body_excerpt:
You don’t usually need a reference list for classics.

If you are using a reference list because you’re citing other works as well, then include the classics you have cited.

If you include a classics work in the reference list, cite the particular translation and edition you are working with. Make sure you:

- specify the date of the edition, not the date of the creation of the work
- acknowledge the translator (‘trans’)
- place the date at the end of the reference list entry – this is contrary to author–date style, but it stops possible confusion caused by, for example, ‘Plato (1954)’
- hyperlink titles in digital content where available.
heading_path: List classics with other references
source.statement: List classics with other references

source.body_excerpt:
Musical compositions include:

- songs
- operas
- ballets
- dances
- chamber music
- soundtracks
- electronic music.

Information about musical compositions can include the:

- title
- common name
- type of composition
- composition’s key
- target instrument or instruments
- catalogue number.

You might use references for musical compositions in the program for official events or other government-sponsored performances, or when using a soundtrack, such as in a video.

The references must be accurate and complete so that they:

- provide all the information someone needs to identify the work properly
- comply with copyright and licensing laws.

Examples of in-text citations and reference lists on this page follow the author–date system, as this is the most common way of citing musical compositions in government content. If your organisation uses the documentary–note system, change the citation and style of reference list accordingly.
heading_path: Cite musical compositions correctly
source.statement: Cite musical compositions correctly

source.body_excerpt: For compositions with no given name, use roman type and no quotation marks. Always use a capital letter for the key of musical compositions.
heading_path: Use roman type for unnamed compositions
source.statement: Use roman type for unnamed compositions

source.body_excerpt: Style for the title of a composition depends on what version you are referring to.
heading_path: Use italics for long works and compilations, roman type for songs
source.statement: Use italics for long works and compilations, roman type for songs

source.body_excerpt:
Write the name of the song, the author and the year of publication in parentheses when you cite lyrics in a text.

If you mention the name of the song in the text, place only the author and the year in parentheses. If you mention the author in text, put the date in parentheses straight after the author’s name.

Use single quotation marks and sentence case for the name of the song.
heading_path: Cite the song when you use someone’s lyrics
source.statement: Cite the song when you use someone's lyrics

source.body_excerpt:
In government content, you don’t need to create a reference list to cite musical compositions. If you have a reference list already, add musical compositions to your list.

If you’re writing another type of content, check whether you need to add musical compositions to a reference list.

Rule: Creator C (Year) ‘Title of song: subtitle of song’ [Medium], *Title of compilation or album*, Name of Publisher.
heading_path: Include musical compositions if you’re using a reference list
source.statement: Include musical compositions if you're using a reference list

source.body_excerpt:
You might need to refer to plays and poetry in information about events, in digital content and in other publications.

References to plays and poetry must be accurate and complete so that they:

- provide all the information someone needs to identify the work properly
- comply with copyright laws.

Examples of in-text citations and reference lists on this page follow the author–date system, as this is the most common way of citing plays and poetry in government content. If your organisation uses the documentary–note system, change the citation and reference list styles accordingly.
heading_path: Cite plays and poems correctly
source.statement: Cite plays and poems correctly

source.body_excerpt: Style for play titles follows the same convention as for books but is based on details about the published edition. Quoted material from plays has distinct punctuation and formatting.
heading_path: Reference play titles and quotes from plays
source.statement: Reference play titles and quotes from plays

source.body_excerpt: Write titles of plays in italics and use sentence case. This means the first word and any proper nouns have an initial capital letter.
heading_path: Reference play titles and quotes from plays
Use italics and sentence case for titles of plays
source.statement: Use italics and sentence case for titles of plays

source.body_excerpt: When you quote lines spoken by a character in a play, use a forward slash to show line breaks appearing in the original. Insert spaces around the forward slash. If there's a line break in your text, it can occur before or after the slash.
heading_path: Reference play titles and quotes from plays
Use a forward slash to show line breaks in plays
source.statement: Use a forward slash to show line breaks in plays

source.body_excerpt: In plays, you don’t need quotation marks if the direct speech follows the name of the speaker.
heading_path: Reference play titles and quotes from plays
Don’t use quotation marks in scripts of plays
source.statement: Don't use quotation marks in scripts of plays

source.body_excerpt:
Citations to plays are more helpful if you use divisions – acts, scenes and lines. Readers who wish to read the quote in context can use the divisions to find it in any edition of the play.

Use the full name of the playwright, unless people can identify the playwright by the surname. Use roman type (not italics), lower case and numerals for divisions.
heading_path: Reference play titles and quotes from plays
Use divisions for in-text citations of plays
source.statement: Use divisions for in-text citations of plays

source.body_excerpt: In government content, you don’t need to create a reference list just to cite plays. If you have a reference list already, then add plays to your list. You can also add reviews of plays to the list.
heading_path: Reference play titles and quotes from plays
Include plays if you’re using a reference list
source.statement: Include plays if you're using a reference list

source.body_excerpt: Style for references to poem titles depends on how the poem was published. Refer to parts of poems using the right kind of punctuation.
heading_path: Reference poem titles and parts of poems
source.statement: Reference poem titles and parts of poems

source.body_excerpt: Enclose titles of poems in quotation marks. If the title is part of a quotation, enclose it in double quotation marks.
heading_path: Reference poem titles and parts of poems
Use quotation marks for titles of poems
source.statement: Use quotation marks for titles of poems

source.body_excerpt:
Poems can be published as a freestanding work in book form. In this case, follow the citation rules for books. Use italics for the poem’s title.

This means you italicise the titles of verse novels as you do for prose novels.
heading_path: Reference poem titles and parts of poems
Italicise titles of poems published as books
source.statement: Italicise titles of poems published as books

source.body_excerpt:
A poem’s title is part of its artistic integrity. Apply the author’s own style for capitalisation and punctuation. If the title is all lower case or all upper case, follow suit.

If you’re unsure of the author’s style, write the titles of poems using sentence case. Sentence case can usually replace title case (maximal capitalisation), which is often a publishing style rather than an artistic choice.
heading_path: Reference poem titles and parts of poems
Capitalise and punctuate the title of a poem as the author does
source.statement: Capitalise and punctuate the title of a poem as the author does

source.body_excerpt:
Filmpoems are a combination of images and poetry (spoken or written) watched on a screen. Filmpoems also include people reciting poetry onscreen. Sometimes filmpoems have other names, such as ‘poetryfilms’, ‘videopoems’ or ‘screen poetry’.

Italicise titles of filmpoems and use the original capitalisation and punctuation.
heading_path: Reference poem titles and parts of poems
Italicise titles of filmpoems
source.statement: Italicise titles of filmpoems

source.body_excerpt:
Some poems do not have titles. They often become known by their first line and are usually cited that way. Even if the poem isn’t well known, use the first line as a title for untitled poems. The aim is to give readers enough information to find the poem.

Use quotation marks as you would for other titles. Capitalise the line as it appears in the poem.
heading_path: Reference poem titles and parts of poems
Use the first lines of untitled, published poems
source.statement: Use the first lines of untitled, published poems

source.body_excerpt: The nature of spoken word and performance poetry means the text often isn’t published. Give people enough information to appreciate and identify the poem. It’s possible a performance was recorded. To help people find it online, name the poet and the event, or quote some of the poet’s words.
heading_path: Reference poem titles and parts of poems
Describe untitled, unpublished spoken word poems
source.statement: Describe untitled, unpublished spoken word poems

source.body_excerpt: If a poem is part of a published collection, italicise the title of the collection and use sentence case. Use quotation marks for the poems in the collection.
heading_path: Reference poem titles and parts of poems
Use italics for titles of anthologies and other collections
source.statement: Use italics for titles of anthologies and other collections

source.body_excerpt: Separate lines of poetry in a sentence with a forward slash. Insert spaces around the forward slash. If there's a line break in your text, it can occur before or after the slash.
heading_path: Reference poem titles and parts of poems
Use a forward slash to show line breaks in poems
source.statement: Use a forward slash to show line breaks in poems

source.body_excerpt:
In government writing, mentioning the poet and the title of the poem is usually enough.

Always cite quotations in text. Follow the quotation with the poet’s name in roman type and the title of the poem in quotation marks. Use the poet’s full name, unless people can identify the poet by the surname alone.
heading_path: Reference poem titles and parts of poems
Use in-text citations for quotations from poems
source.statement: Use in-text citations for quotations from poems

source.body_excerpt:
Use lower case and numerals for divisions.
